Anantaśayana Sanskrit Series, Volume 60: Laghustutiḥ
Composed by the venerable Laghubhaṭṭāraka,
accompanied by the commentary composed by Śrī Rāghavānanda, [edited] by the Director of the Sanskrit Text Publication Project.
It was edited by Ta. Gaṇapati Śāstrin,
and it...
By the command of the Great King Mahāmahima Śrīmūlaka Rāmavarman, the crest-jewel of his lineage, at Anantaśayana,
this was printed at the royal printing press under its director.
Printed and published.
Śrīḥ.
The *Laghustuti* composed by the venerable Laghubhaṭṭāraka, together with the commentary composed by Śrī Rāghavānanda.

May she who is the singular embodiment of consciousness transcending the universe, yet who shines here as the very soul of the universe; she who is constantly worshipped by those of meritorious deeds who have destroyed the delusions of duality;
she whom I, afflicted by the sufferings of saṃsāra, serve with trust and a heart [thinking] "I am she"—may she protect me.
Is it not that the beloved of Maheśa has taken us—who are otherwise without refuge—under her feet?

The venerable Mallaghubhaṭṭāraka himself, having attained the state of the supreme consciousness— the realization of identity with the supreme consciousness known by the other name of the "descent of the supreme power" (para-śaktipāta)— obtained through the compassionate glance of his preeminent guru, whom he had propitiated with sincere devotion.

With the entire web of the noose of defects completely destroyed and supreme bliss manifested, may others also attain the state of supreme consciousness through this hymn which illuminates the specific majesty of the manifestations of the reality of the Supreme Deity;
for, due to ignorance of that [reality], they remain in the ocean of suffering beginning with birth and ending with death.
Beholding those submerged [in worldly existence] through the analogy of his own self, his heart overwhelmed with compassion, he offers praise while aspiring for their blessing:
"Bearing a radiance upon her forehead like that of Indra’s bow..."
Spreading a white luster everywhere from her head like that of the cool-rayed moon,
this very Tripurā— like the light of the sun always residing within the heart—
is composed of light and speech; may she suddenly sever your sin with her three steps.
p.
2) "Like that of Indra," etc. The introduction [to a work] consists of either a benediction, a salutation, or a statement of the subject matter.
Thus, the benediction recited first here at the beginning follows the path of propriety;

the statement of the subject matter (*vastunirdeśa*) is made solely as a supplement to it. By this, both the subject matter of this jewel of a hymn—the form of the mantra-deity—is revealed, as well as its purpose, characterized by immediate liberation (*sadyomukti*).

It is being elucidated: here, all beings (*paśu*) are bound by the noose of *māyā* and their bodies are tormented by the threefold suffering. Among them, even those humans who, for the sake of ritual injunction (*vidhi*) or by mere whim, kill animals—all of them are understood to be qualified [for this practice] provided they possess devotion to the Guru and the Deity; this is known from the general designation [of the rule]. As it has been said:
"One who has fallen away from all other means should take refuge in the path of the Kula.

Thus, by virtue of its universal eligibility, the extreme purity and great fruitfulness of this Stotra-tantra are revealed, like the flow of the Bhāgīrathī, the Bhāratī, and other rivers. [May it remove] your sin (*agham*).

By the phrasing "one should cut," he reveals his own state as the Lord of the Self, since he has himself fulfilled all desires and thus has solely the welfare of others as his purpose; by this, this *stotra-tantra* may be accepted by all as being intrinsically authoritative (*svataḥ-pramāṇa*).

Indeed, no man of merit would ever intentionally descend into the Vaitaraṇī river of speech— though he be born of the lineage of Vasiṣṭha, a preeminent twice-born purified by forty sacraments, yet still bound by a multitude of fetters, with the divine state unmanifested, and his desires unfulfilled. But as for him who...
One does not become a slayer of the self. Although this has been extensively explained by former masters through both summary and detail,

it is nevertheless like the waters of the Bhāgīrathī or the Bhāratī, which, though served by people of antiquity, are [drunk] by contemporary men who have entered upon the path of their own purification under the name of Rāghavānanda, a preeminent sage.

For one's own purification, it is practiced and investigated according to one's capacity through both concise and detailed methods. Here, *vṛtta* (meter) is of two kinds: *mātrāvṛtta* (meter by syllabic instants) and *varṇavṛtta* (meter by syllables). Among these, where five *gaṇas* (metrical feet) are arranged with four *mātrās* each, verses (*ślokas*) are formed by them.
Verses composed by grouping [syllables] according to their measure (*tanmātrāvṛtta*) are, for example, the *pathyā-āryā* and others.
On the other hand, where one constructs eight groups (*gaṇa*) consisting of three syllables each and composes a verse based upon them,
that is a *varṇavṛtta*.

And therein, among the meters beginning with *uktā* and *atyuktā*, which consist of four feet measured by a sequence starting from one syllable per foot and increasing by one syllable for each subsequent foot, up to the *utkṛti* class;
The introduction of verses ending with twenty-six syllables occurs [here]. Beyond that, there are the *daṇḍaka* meters beginning with *caṇḍavṛṣṭipravāha*.
Among them, in the meter known as *atidhṛti*, which consists of a verse of nineteen syllables, there are metrical patterns.
This collection of verses, composed in the meter known as Śārdūlavikrīḍita, takes the form of a hymn of praise.

Herein, this opening verse introduces the nature of the Tripurā mantra and its deity. Following that, two [verses] concern the reality characterized by the deity of the first seed-syllable (bīja), primarily through the prominence of the *nāda* and *bindu*, and primarily through the prominence of the seed-syllable itself.
And [the remaining two] reveal the fruits of service: the fourth has the purpose of [revealing] the fruit of service to the deity of its second seed-syllable;
the fifth follows upon the fruit of service to the deity of the third seed-syllable;
and the sixth is the proclaimer of the fruit of the sequence of reciting that mantra.

The seventh [verse] illuminates the fruit of meditating on the deity common to those three seed-mantras (*bīja*). Following that, three verses concern the fruit of meditating on the deities of each individual seed-mantra. The eleventh establishes the fruit of meditating on the partless syllable (*niṣkalākṣara*) residing in the second seed-mantra. The twelfth [verse concerns] the practice of this.
The thirteenth [verse] indicates that the visible fruit consists of the sovereignty of omniscience and so forth;

it declares that for worldly beings, even with infinite other means, the experience of enjoyment and liberation in this very life is difficult to attain without practicing this. The fourteenth [verse] makes known the specific qualifications, means, and fruits of its practice. The fifteenth...

The sixteenth is the instructor of the Goddess’s form that transcends phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca*); he is the helmsman who determines the form consisting of the phenomenal world made up of both word and meaning. The seventeenth is the name of a particular manifestation of the Supreme Sovereign (*Parameśvarī*) to be meditated upon by those desiring specific results.
He instructs as follows: the eighteenth concerns the recitation (*pārāyaṇa*) of its mantra;

the nineteenth concerns the recitation of its names; and the twentieth concerns this hymn (*stotra*) by virtue of its subject matter being the consciousness of Tripura and its being composed of mantra itself.
This [work] proclaims that it is to be practiced by the virtuous.

Because it has appeared suddenly, without contradiction, and with full awareness— even from one such as myself of little learning— solely through the power of the grace of the Guru and the Deity, it should be accepted as self-evident authority (*svataḥ-pramāṇa*), like this very scripture.
The Great Souls (mahātman) support this point as follows:

This is the concise summary of the entire essence of the meaning of the hymn. Now, the meaning of each individual verse will also be explained there in due order. This [reality], which is experienced by all people in the form of the manifold duality consisting of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge—

Furthermore, she is not separated by space, time, or other such conditions; for she is the locus of the manifestation and concealment of all this [universe], devoid of distinctions such as the knower and so forth, and her nature transcends the world-complex (prapañca) which consists of undivided consciousness. For this very reason, her true essence is unseen by anyone who lacks devotion to her. She is characterized by three cities (pur), which serve as her abodes.
For this very reason, the Goddess, who is renowned as Tripurā because she possesses three cities (*pura*), [destroys] for you— her own worshippers— the evil (*agha*),
which consists solely of ignorance regarding the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) and is threefold, being divided into the *āṇava*, *māyīya*, and *kārmika* types.

The connection [of the words] is as follows: one should cut through impurity suddenly—that is, in a short time—and always by means of the emptiness of re-arising; having become manifest through one's own self, one should withdraw it. And thus says the scripture:
"The supreme Speech, which does not depart, is indeed the light of one's own nature within."
In which, when its true nature has been perceived, one's qualification [for further practice] ceases.
Thus [it is said]. This should be construed with the phrase "in her whose true nature has been seen within. And the *Bhagavadgītā* states:
"Knowledge is veiled by ignorance; thereby living beings are deluded.
But for those whose ignorance has been destroyed by knowledge of the Self..."
Their knowledge illumines that Supreme like the sun;
their intellects are absorbed in That, their very selves are That, they are established in That, and That is their ultimate goal.
Those whose impurities have been shaken off by knowledge go to the state from which there is no return.

Thus it is said. What is its essential nature? To this it is replied: "consisting of light" (*jyotirmayī*) and "consisting of speech" (*vāṅmayī*). That uninterrupted self-reflection (*ahaṃvimarśa*), which is the very nature of the Supreme Lord—the Self of all beings whose sole body is luminosity—is designated by the term "light. As it is stated in the *Rahasyāgama*: "The Goddess Tripurā is one's own consciousness."

Characterized by the reflective awareness and verbal expression of that [reality], consisting of the contraction of all phonemes from 'a' to 'ha', and being the essence of the entire sacred tradition,
I am the letter 'a' among letters and the dual compound among all compounds.

Thus, according to the principle stated in the *Śrī Bhagavad Gītā* and the principle stated by the Teacher that "the one known as *ahaṃ* (I) becomes the pervasive *prakṛti*," the word *ahaṃ*— which possesses the phonemic form of the letters *a* and *ha* joined as a copulative compound (*dvandva-samāsa*), having attained the neuter gender and singular number— is renowned as the Great Mantra (*mahāmantra*) because it is the imperishable Supreme (*parā*).

That which is grasped by the word "speech" is the Self itself, according to the Vedic revelation: "I am Brahman. He who perceives the Self directly by means of the Self through the state of full I-consciousness, and not through artificial egoism—he truly sees.

And thus it is stated in the venerable *Anuttara-nirṇaya*: "In this way, this very [reality], consisting of light and consisting of speech, is in its partial aspect the Heart of the Supreme Lord—both immanent as the soul of the universe and transcendent beyond it. (p. 5)
We praise consciousness, which flashes forth in the form of the supreme primordial power (parā-ādi-śakti).

Thus, the meaning of the secret tradition has been revealed. This very [deity], whose supreme and non-supreme forms are presented here, is well-known not only in the Āgamas but also in the Upaniṣads—as in: "The all-pervading, supreme, eternal Nārāyaṇa, Hari, who is the universe."
Thus, in the seventh chapter of the Bhagavad Gītā: "Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind,
intellect, and ego— thus is my material nature divided eightfold."
But know, O mighty-armed one, that there is another, higher nature of Mine,
which is the life-force by which this entire world is sustained.
And so forth, in the thirteenth chapter:
"O son of Kuntī! This body is called the 'field' (kṣetra).
He who knows this, those who know the truth call him the 'knower of the field' (kṣetrajña)."

When this and more has been taught by the teachers and supported in the *Prapañcasāra* by such passages as "Nature (*prakṛti*) and the Person (*puruṣa*) are indeed eternal," and so forth— then, in response to the inquiry as to by what rite the Goddess might become intent upon severing the bond, [the author] proceeds to reveal the means, the object of worship, the locus, and the instruments thereof.
He describes the three steps of the Goddess as consisting of light and speech with the words beginning "of Indra":
situated in the middle of the forehead—that is, in the center of the forehead at the location of the *ājñā*—she possesses a radiance like that of Indra’s bow;
she resides in the lotus of the heart.

The meaning is that she is to be meditated upon by means of the *kāmabīja* (the seed-syllable of desire), her form consisting of mere radiant energy that is white, red, and black, extending as far as the lotus between the eyebrows, and possessing three limbs. She spreads a whiteness like the luster of the moon—which is not hot—over all directions from the twelve-petaled lotus at the crown of the head; thus she is pervaded while residing in the *ājñā*-lotus.

That which possesses a form of radiance resembling the light of the moon is to be worshipped by means of the seed-syllable of Śakti; that is to say, she resides in the heart, within the lotus of the heart. Situated like the rising splendor of the sun, the hot-rayed one, her light extending from the lotus of the *mūlādhāra* up to the lotus of the heart, she is of the nature of a brilliance resembling the rising sun.

That is to say, one should worship [Her] by means of the *vāgbhava* [seed-syllable]. As it has been stated in the *Śrīsaubhāgyahṛdaya*: "O Great Goddess, Your light is like a mass of gold in the *yonisthāna*, blazing with flashes of lightning in the heart, and resembling the moon in the *ājñācakra*."
Thus [ends] the manner of praise. As for the method of extracting the mantra—wherein it is clearly stated in the first verse:
"The procedure for extracting the mantra is declared by means of the number of syllables in its quarters, following the sequence of one, two, and three quarters," at the conclusion.

Because they will be explained [later], the seed-syllables of the venerable Bālā have been extracted in this verse from the first, second, and third syllables of the first, second, and third quarters respectively. In the word *sarvataḥ*, the *visarga* has also been extracted before the letter *sau*; since the *sakāra* arises from that [visarga], it is extracted as well. Thus, "from all" (*sarvataḥ*).

By the inclusion of the long vowel *ṛ* (tapara), even that which was not previously mentioned has been extracted. By the separate treatment of those two, the distinction between the pure (*śuddha*) and other types is indicated.

Since it was stated, "The procedure for extracting mantras along with their specific details has been told," their specific variations are extracted right here. How so? *ai ī au*; *aiṃ ī au*; *aiṃ īṃ au*; *aiṃ īṃ auḥ*. Thus.

The pure non-dualities are included right here and are therefore extracted together [with them]. Thus, they are always situated in the *A* and *Ha*; they rest upon the head of the moon (*anuṣṇagu*) and the bindu, and because of this, they possess a radiance that shines everywhere, bearing the splendor of the power of the delineation of Great Light and Contemplation (*vimarśa*). And thus, they constitute the seed-syllable of all mantras.

The Great Mantra is extracted: *haiṃ klīṃ hsauḥ*. Because she resides everywhere (*sarvataḥ*) within all seed-syllables (*bīja*) and is established in the letter *ha*, this is the extraction of the mantra of Tripurāvāsinī. *hai hī hsau*: because she exists suddenly (*sahasā*) everywhere through the letters *ha* and *sa*, this is the Śrīmantra of the Middle Four-Peaked Tripurā.

*Hsaiṃ hsklīṃ hsauḥ*. She who dwells eternally with the burning [flame] (*sadāha*) by force (*sahasā*), and in whom resides the fire (*vahni*) possessing the quality of burning (*dāhaguṇa*)—that is, she who dwells in that letter *ra*: this is the mantra of the goddess Tripurā, consisting of five middle peaks (*pañcakūṭa*). *Hsraiṃ hsklrīṃ hsrauḥ*. She who dwells everywhere and eternally with the burning [flame] by force; *klīṃ*, she whose form consists of the letters *ka* and *la*, [bestowing] splendor (*kānti*).

And "spreading a cause of beauty" refers to the mantra of the Siddha of Tripura consisting of all five *kūṭas*: *hsklraiṃ hsklarīṃ hsklraiḥ*. In that very context, upon the head of the letter *go* (the letter *u*) which is not hot (*anuṣṇaga*), and with the letter *ḍa* situated above as the causal sign, it is that which spreads splendor and radiance in every direction; thus, it is the essence of the glorious twelve-and-a-half *kūṭas*.
The mantra of Tripurāmbikā is: *hsklrḍai*, *hsklrdī*, *hsklrdauḥ*. These four are accompanied by the letter *sa* (*sādayaḥ*).

[The mantras] begin with *śai*, *śklīṃ*, *śauḥ*, and so forth. Likewise, the six mantras beginning with Bālā may end in the visarga, end in the bindu, end in both the bindu and the visarga, or be devoid of both. This and other such details should be inferred according to what is heard in the scriptures.

All vowels are manifested from the first seed-syllable and the final seed-syllable of the *bāla* [alphabet], ending with the *bindu* and *visarga*. How so? Through the combination of the qualities (*guṇa*) of the *i*-vowels and the *a*-vowels, the vowel *e* arises. Furthermore, through the combination of the *vṛddhi* of the *e*-vowel with the *a*-vowels, the vowel *ai* arises. And likewise:
p.

7) The six vowels—*a*, *ā*, *i*, *ī*, *e*, and *ai*—as well as the fifteenth vowel in the form of the *bindu*, are included within the first seed-syllable (*bīja*). Likewise, through the application of *guṇa* [vowel-strengthening], the vowel *o* arises from the two sounds *u* and *ava*; of that...

Furthermore, by the addition of the vowel *u* to the letter *a*, the sound *au* is formed. Thus, the remaining vowels—*u*, *ū*, *o*, and *au*—along with the visarga, which consists of sixteen vowels, are included within the final seed-syllable (*bīja*). The two vowels *ṛ* and *ṝ* are merely different forms of the letter *ra*, while *ḷ* and *ḹ* are forms of the letter *la*. The visarga, when pronounced in reverse order, is the letter *ha*.

And the letter *ka* is in the middle seed-syllable. Therefore, by the principle of "enclosure" (*sandamśanyāya*), all the consonants are included by taking the first and last letters. By means of the letters *sa* and *ka*, the letter *kṣa* is also taken up. Thus, the *mātṛkā* consisting of fifty letters is extracted here. And in the extraction of the *mātṛkā*:

All mantras, yantras, tantras, Vedas, śāstras, itihāsas, purāṇas, kāvyas, nāṭakas, varieties of languages, varieties of songs, and varieties of hymns are indicated [within this], because everything is composed of that. For this very reason it has been said:
"There is no mantra higher than Mātṛkā. Thus, in the third seed-syllable, *su au jas* is the form of the nominative case.

It is obtained; and since that [meaning] rests solely upon the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the six case-endings beginning with the accusative (*dvitīyā*) are included within this very [meaning]. This is because the meaning of the nominal stem itself, when possessing its various specific states, exists as the factors of action (*kāraka*) such as the object (*karman*) and so forth. In this way, even the seven case-endings are contained within it.

In the *Tripurā* [mantra], these are extracted by means of the final seed-syllable (*bīja*). Furthermore, the thirty-one principles beginning with Earth (*pṛthivī*) and ending with Māyā are here grasped by the letter *sa*, which is all-pervasive due to its perception as "existent" (*sat-sat*).
And by the letter *au*, the five principles beginning with Śuddhavidyā and ending with Śiva are grasped.

Because it arises from the power (*śakti*) of the upward-expansion of unsurpassed bliss, and because it is itself a specific power (*śaktiviśeṣa*) by virtue of being the possessor of those parts (*avayavin*), it consists of five powers. And these, ultimately, are none other than the powers of consciousness (*cit*), bliss (*ānanda*), will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*).
They consist of the five principles beginning with Śiva and ending with Śuddhavidyā. Furthermore, the thirty-six principles shine forth within the final seed-syllable (*bīja*). As it has been said:
"Just as a great tree exists in the form of a potentiality within the seed of a *nyagrodha* tree..."
In this way, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings resides within the seed-syllable of the heart.

Thus, by means of the *visarga* in the form of a point (*bindu*) above and below, the primary reality known as Paramaśiva-Parābhaṭṭārikā—which is the locus for the manifestation and withdrawal of all principles (*tattva*)—is also subsumed; this is the general direction [of the teaching].
In this way, she is called Tripurā because she is endowed with three locations, forms, and seed-syllables (*bīja*), which are synonymous with "prior" (*pura*).

This is the etymological derivation (*nirukta*). And this is also an indication of other derivations. How so? Because she existed prior to the three—fire, water, and food—she is *Tripurā*. "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1).

"Only one, without a second—that [Being] thought: 'Let me become many,' it emitted heat; it emitted water; that [water] emitted food"—so says the Śruti. Furthermore, because of its threefold nature beginning with heat, or because the effect does not exist apart from the cause, [the Śruti says]:
"The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is the reality. And thus, my dear, is that instruction. So too says the Śruti.

Likewise, because it existed prior to the three worlds, or because it has their nature; or because it existed prior to the three Vedas, or because it has their nature; or because it existed prior to the three gods, or because it has their nature;
or because it existed prior to the sun, fire, and moon, or because it has their nature; or because it existed prior to the knower and so forth.
"Because of existence, or because of having that form, prior to the three powers, because of existence, or because of having that form," and so forth.

Here, the Great Mantra is "prior" (purā) to this very one called Tripura, because there are three seed-syllables (bīja) consisting of the forms of Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī. Here, [it belongs] to the innermost Self of all.

The first [consciousness] consists of the undivided reflective awareness of the "I" (*ahantā*) of the Supreme Lord, which is imperishable. The second consists of the reflective awareness of the "I" as delimited by the body and so forth. The third consists of the reflective awareness of "this-ness" (*idantā*) directed toward objects such as blue or pleasure—which are distinct from the body and the subjects of the *māyā*-state—while remaining within one's own self.

The distinction is that the fourth [verse] consists of its expansion. The omission of the phrase "with three cities" (*puraiḥ*) and the inclusion of the phrase "with three words" (*padaiḥ*) are for the purpose of identifying the Vedic revelation; the Vedic text beginning with "Speech is measured in four quarters" (*catvāri vāk parimitā padāni*) should be reflected upon here. In this hymn, the word *tripurā* denotes the deity, whereas elsewhere it denotes the mantra.
It should be observed. || 1 ||

Having thus taught the mantras, deities, places of worship, and fruits of the practice of Tripurā in general, he now desires to teach their specific details; first, regarding the deity who exists in three ways— by way of the divisions of *nāda*, *bindu*, and *bīja*—
and who abides in the first *bīja* through the threefold division of *niṣkala*, *sakalaniṣkala*, and *sakala*:

He describes his majesty with two verses: "We consider that measure which, ever residing in your first seed-syllable (*vāgbīja*), rivals the rising of the extremely fine thread of the *trapusī* creeper; that [measure], we [meditate upon] as yours."
Having thus understood that Śakti, known as Kuṇḍalinī, is intent upon the exertion of generating the universe, men no longer experience childhood within a mother’s womb.

"Yā mātrā" (that which is the measure): by the first [line] of these two, he describes how the fruit of the worship of the *bindu*—which is accompanied by the *sana* and the deity—is indeed the destruction of sin (*aghaccheda*). Although the destruction of sin was [already mentioned] in the previous verse regarding Tripurā...

Although [liberation] has been taught as the fruit of mantra in general, nevertheless this undertaking is for the purpose of considering the fruit of its specific [form]; thus it is taught that the fruit of the worship of *sanādabindu* is indeed liberation (*mokṣa*). The address "O Goddess" (*devī*) should be understood here as well, from the subsequent verse.

The Goddess (Devī) is so called because she sports within her own self through the fivefold acts characterized by the creation, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, and grace of the universe; or because her nature is self-luminous consciousness.
Thus is her address. Alternatively, [it refers to] the God (Dev), the Great God (Mahādeva), whose singular essence is self-luminosity, who is the inner self of all.
The Goddess consists of the unconditioned self-reflexive awareness (*aham-vimarśa*) which is Her very nature;

or rather, She is the illuminator of the subject of *māyā*— characterized by the void, intellect, vital breath, and body— and of the objects within it, such as pleasure, pain, blue, yellow, and so forth, as well as the cognitions of those objects, manifesting them in the form of "I," "mine," and so on, by virtue of the penetration of their own inherent light.

The Goddess: [She who is] situated within the first seed-syllable (*bīja*) related to you—that is, pertaining to you—known as the *vāgbhava* (speech-born) seed, which is triangular in shape, consisting of the central womb (*yoni*) among the nine wombs located in the pericarp of the four-petaled lotus at the *mūlādhāra*.
She resides in its center, having the form of the *nāda* and the *bindu*; she is that *mātrā*, that digit of power.

The Kuṇḍalinī Śakti, as is well known in the scriptures, is like the rising thread from the body of the trapusī creeper—that is, the urvāru vine; it is similar to, and possesses the same configuration and luminous form as, that shimmering thread which rises from its body, being a fine strand with a rounded tip. [One should contemplate] her.

Having known her— who is intent on the activity of creating the universe, who takes the forms of Parā, Paśyantī, and the rest, and who, through the sequence of the fifty phonemes, gives birth to the manifold expansion of words and meanings— and having worshipped her as one's own self at all three daily libations (savanas), men shall no longer [experience] that state of being an embryo situated within the womb of a mother.
They do not touch [you], for they themselves have attained the state of being the progenitor and progenitress of the universe; thus we think, we conclude: "We are your devotees. || 2 ||

Having thus stated that the meditation on *sanāda-bindu* has liberation as its fruit, he describes— by way of the *kaimutika-nyāya* (the logic of "how much more so")— that the fruit of meditating on the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is the attainment of mastery over speech, which is the most effective means for achieving the knowledge that leads to that [liberation]: "Upon seeing an object that causes agitation, one suddenly utters 'Ai Ai!'"

O Giver of Boons! O Goddess! for one who, even here through the power of unintentional [utterance], pronounces a syllable even without the *bindu*, when your grace has swiftly arisen for him, it is indeed certain.
From the interior of the mouth, words issue forth, shedding the liquid essence of the nectar of well-spoken verses.

"Seeing [something] with agitation" means: "O Giver of Boons (varade)!"—addressing her as such because she grants the entirety of the desired objects cherished by the practitioner. "In this world," when a person suddenly and unexpectedly sees an object that causes agitation, such as a snake, then, by the force of intention—that is, due to another underlying purpose or even for reasons such as fear—[he acts].

When even the first syllable "ai ai" was uttered without the nasal dot (bindu), by virtue of Your grace having arisen, it was as if one were touched by fire—even against one's will—according to the maxim: "Fire indeed burns. Thus, when Your sidelong glance has fallen, [the words] immediately and swiftly emit the flowing essence of the nectar of well-spoken verses.
"Excellent sayings" (*sūktayaḥ*) are well-characterized and very sweet utterances; they are like the flowing liquid of the essence of nectar (*sudhārasadrava*), for they emit that [nectar].
Such words indeed issue forth from the interior of the mouth, manifesting of their own accord.
This is certainly certain (*dhruvam*). What [more] can be said of one who practices the black seed-syllable (*kṛṣṇabīja*) according to the prescribed rule with the sole desire for that?
The meaning is "again" (punar) as well. || 3 ||

Likewise, regarding the second seed-syllable as well, with the intention that even a single part possesses the nature of Sarasvatī, let alone the whole, he says: "O Eternal One! If some rare wise man on earth understands that the other syllable of the mantra, Kāmarāja, is the partless (niṣkala) Sarasvatī..."
The twice-born, proclaiming this narrative of Satyatapas at the beginning of every section, clearly utter it after first placing it within the syllable Om, the abode of the Pranava.

Regarding the phrase "O Eternal One": O Eternal One! O You whose nature is consciousness, uninterrupted throughout the three periods of time! That which is called *Kāmarāja*—the second syllable of the mantra—which is *niṣkala*, meaning devoid even of the letters *ka* and *la*; if anyone on earth knows that it is *sārasvata*, causing the grace of Sarasvatī, he is rare and few indeed.
Even a child becomes wise. Why? By reciting the narrative of the seer Satyatapas at every parvan and on every new moon day—those twice-born ones who proclaim that syllable (p.

When the *praṇava* itself is the locus— the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*)— of that which is fond of the locus of the *praṇava*, [they] utter it clearly and loudly at the beginning, having made it consist of only this much, namely the syllable *īṃ*. This is because it shares the same meaning and the same purpose as the *praṇava*.

Thus, it is stated that the fruit is the realization of the reality (*tattva*) of Tripurasarasvatī. And so says the Śruti: "He who has abandoned the companion who knows the truth—for him there is no portion even in speech.
Even if he hears, he hears in vain; for he does not know the path of righteous action. The meaning of this is as follows:

Even regarding speech, there is a specific seed-mantra (*mantrabīja*). A "companion" (*sakhā*) is one who is conjoined with, eternally connected to, and shares the same knowledge; he proclaims—that is, fully explains—the specific meaning.
That companion is the phoneme which is recited as a unity and established in a single purpose. He who abandons—that is, leaves behind—his portion belongs to those who recite it.

That fruit does not exist at all; he demonstrates this very point by way of illustration with the words "yadi īm" (if [one hears] *īm*). He who hears this form consisting of the syllable *īm*—that is, receives it from the presence of a teacher—if he hears it as *alaka*, meaning devoid of the letters *ka* and *la*, and grasps it as the mantra simply as *īm*, then:

He does not know—that is, he does not experience—the path, the way, the fruit of merit consisting in the subjugation of the three worlds, which arises from the recitation of the seed-syllable of desire for well-performed deeds;
rather, he becomes truly liberated from the bondage characterized by the perception of the entire manifold of duality. By means of this *praṇava*...

Because they share a single purpose, their possession of a single fruit is inevitable. That state of having a single purpose is ascertained from the fact that at the beginning of the narrative of Satyatapas, he alone was consecrated by all the Brāhmaṇas in the position of the *tāra*. Furthermore, the *praṇava* is taught in the Upaniṣads as having liberation as its sole fruit and the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) as its sole object.
"Meditate upon the Self as 'Om' alone; abandon other words, for this is the bridge to immortality.

Whatever one hears of this, even if one hears it indistinctly, then [one finds] the path of all good deeds, of all merit—even the station of Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, and the rest. Indeed, he does not know [it] well; he does not know much.

He carries [it] away; the meaning is that he experiences the bliss of Brahman right here in this very world. Alternatively, he does not even know the path of good deeds, much less the path of evil deeds;
the meaning is that, being devoid of both together with their fruits, he becomes liberated.
Salutation to that Self of liberation, toward whom peaceful renunciants— freed from the fear of rebirth— proceed upon the cessation of both demerit and merit.

Thus [it is said]. Or else, if he hears this *alarka* [song], then for him whose "good deeds" (*sukṛta*)—that is, the beautiful acts of sacrifice, charity, and austerity—are such that all his virtuous works have become fruitful; for him... [p.

"Path" means a track, a course, or a way; or it refers to the body or conduct. The meaning is that no one here knows this [Self], for it would be as if he were seeing something never seen before. This is because of the Vedic revelation: "He attains all that whatever good deeds creatures perform, he who knows what he knows. Thus, the fruit of all actions is the knowledge of Brahman.

The intention is that this [dispassion] arises even in this very life for one who practices it, because hearing the Vedānta and other such means yield visible results; and there is a traditional saying (smṛti):
"Among thousands of men, scarcely one strives for perfection."
Even among those who strive and have attained perfection, only some know me in truth.
Thus [ends section] 4.

Now, regarding the fruit of the worship of the third seed-syllable: I bow in my mind to that third seed-syllable of yours, which shines with the luster of the moon and whose power is seen by the wise to instantly bring about the flow of speech.
May Aurobindo also follow the Sarasvatī to dispel the waters of dullness;
may he be like the word "go" which, when applied to a mountain, invariably bestows success even without the presence of a cow.

Regarding the word *yat*: here too, the vocative case ending *-e* (as in *nitye*) should be understood. *Yat* means that which [is effective] immediately or after a short time. *Vacasām pravṛttikaraṇe* means in the production of speech or in the composition of poetry. *Budhair dṛṣṭaprabhāvam* means its power or efficacy has been witnessed by the wise.
And *yac cenduprabham* refers to that which expresses a form of splendor resembling the light of the moon. *Tārtīyam* means the third.
This is Your seed-syllable; I bow to it always. To the question "For what purpose?", it is said: "astvityādi" (beginning with "astu").
The word-division is as follows: *astu auḥ vaḥ api sarasvatīm anugataḥ jāḍyāmbuvicchittaye gauḥ śabdaḥ giri vartate saḥ niyatam yaḥ gaṃ vinā siddhidaḥ*.
That sound which, having become the word "gauḥ," resides in the mountain (*giri*)—that is, in Sarasvatī—is certainly the bestower of perfection even without the letter *gaṃ*.
It functions invariably and is a definitive designator; that which, without the letter *ga*,
becomes a specific mantra that bestows success and propitiates Sarasvatī— these four diphthong mantras are the accomplishers of all aims.

According to the statement of the Teacher (*ācārya*), the word *va* refers to the Goddess by means of the pronoun *yuṣmad*. "Of you" (*vaḥ*) means belonging to you; [the syllable] *auḥ* follows Sarasvatī, who resides within the third seed-syllable of the Goddess.
May even the word "Aur" serve to cut through the waters of dullness and to destroy the flood of delusion. (The use of the *loṭ* suffix here has the sense of the *liṅ*;

it is used in the sense of an injunction, implying: "it must certainly come to pass," with certainty in the mind. As for the form with the letter *s*, it carries the meaning "how much more so. Thus, with these four verses beginning with "That which is called Mātṛ," [the Goddess] is pure.

The [three seed-syllables] are taught separately as *aiṃ*, *īṃ*, and *auḥ*. I do not accept the third seed-syllable as having mere poetic skill as its fruit, because that is an inseparable consequence of it; rather, my intention is that I accept it as having the cessation of ignorance—the seed of all misfortune—as its fruit. || 5 ||
Furthermore, as to how these seed-syllables (*bīja*) are to be recited—by whom they are to be recited and for what purposes—the text says:

"O Goddess! each one of your seed-syllables is sinless, whether with its consonants and vowels, or standing as a *kūṭa* (consonant cluster), or separately, or following the sequential order, or even arranged out of order."
Whatever desire one contemplates, by whatever method, or whatever [mantra] one meditates upon or recites, it swiftly brings all of that to fruition for men.

Regarding the phrase "each one": O Goddess! each individual seed-syllable belonging to you may be with a consonant (*savyañjana*) or without a consonant (*avyañjana*). Even when it is with a consonant, it may be a *kūṭastha* (an uncombined single consonant), or joined with two or more consonants up to six. Furthermore, even in that case, it may be separate for each, or, if not separate, it may occur according to its sequential order.

Or else, it may be arranged out of sequence; having regard for whatever desire— be it dharma or the like— and by whatever method or procedure, whether by the sequence of the placement of the limbs (*aṅga-nyāsa*) and so forth,
or by the sequence of merely remembering the sandals of the female Guru, or even without performing anything at all, [one attains it] in one's own true form.

Whether it has been recited as the form of the deity expressed by its own mantra, or meditated upon as partless (*niṣkala*), as both with and without parts (*sakala-niṣkala*), or as having parts (*sakala*); for all men— meaning for all human beings, including women, Śūdras, and so forth,
and not only for Brāhmaṇas, wandering ascetics, and the like— it grants that very desire, that sought-after object.
"Entirely" means without exception. "Swiftly" means that he makes [the mantra] fruitful in this very birth, whether it has been recited or meditated upon;
this is stated with the intention that the mantra and its deity are one. As the scripture says:
"Contemplating the oneness of the deity, the guru, and the mantra with one's own self..."

Thus [it is said]. The reason for its universal eligibility (*sarvādhikāritva*) is that it is "flawless" (*anagha*). The sense is that, because it is inherently pure like the water of the Bhāgīrathī, it is fitting that it should be served by all. Here, the four previously mentioned divisions of pure [mantra] have been stated;
furthermore, the six beginning with Kalasundarī have been revealed. And among those, by way of the divisions such as the pure *bindu* and so forth...

"Fourfold" means twenty-four divisions. Within that, since each group of four *kūṭas* beginning with *sa-ādi* and *ha-ādi* is twofold, they have eight divisions. And within each of those, there is a fourfold division.

There are forty [syllables], and there are four pure varieties; thus, there are forty-four mantras. Among them, when reciting the three seed-syllables individually, there is no consideration of sequence or non-sequence. Each of the seed-syllables, such as *bāla* and the others, possesses fourfold variety according to the divisions of the pure (*śuddha*) and so forth. In each of the *kūṭas* consisting of two or more syllables, there is the quality of beginning with *ha* (*hāditva*).

And the state of being "accomplished" (sāditva) should also be understood there. When it is the recitation of the aggregate, then in the process of emanation (sṛṣṭi), the recitation follows the sequence; in maintenance (sthiti) and withdrawal (saṃhāra), it is without sequence. In that regard, when it ends with the first seed-syllable from the end, it is withdrawal; when it ends with the second seed-syllable, it is maintenance. With this in mind, those who know the ancient lore have said:
The first is the beginningless beginning, the middle is the middling-middling, and the end is the endless end; Tripurā bestows swift accomplishment.
Thus it is said:

Ādinātha is the seer (ṛṣi) of these [mantras], the *laipeya* is declared to be the meter (chanda), and the deity is the goddess Tripurā; the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) are formed by repeating her own [syllables] twice.
For those desiring success in speech regarding the Dharma, the sequence of emanation (sṛṣṭikrama) should be used in recitation;
for those seeking wealth and desire, the sequence of maintenance (sthitikrama) is praised by the virtuous in recitation.
For all those seeking liberation, however, the sequence of withdrawal has been taught;
they know this same principle to apply even in the ritual procedure for the placement of the syllables of the mantra.

Aiṃ! O Egg-born (Aṇḍaja) Aṅgajānandadevī! Indeed, how shall I worship your command? Aiṃ! Salutation to the lineage of the venerable Guru’s sandals belonging to Parā. Klīṃ! To Aparā; Sauḥ! To Parāparā; Aiṃ! O Infinite Bliss Lord Anantanandanātha! O Infinite Bliss Goddess Anantanandanāthadevī! Salutation to the sandals of the venerable Guru. Klīṃ.

O Lord God Avatāranātha! O Goddess Avatāranāthadevī! Salutation to the sandals of the venerable Guru (śrīgurupāduka)! Sauḥ! O Lord God Siddhanātha! O Goddess Siddhanāthadevī! Salutation to the sandals of the venerable Guru! Again, [the mantra] is joined with the words for the sandals of the supreme guru (paramaguru) and the feet of the goddess; again, [it is joined with] the sandals of one's own guru—thus [there are] nine.

The sandals of the venerable Guru (śrīgurupādukā) are to be known here as follows: Aiṃ, salutation to the two red feet. Sauḥ, salutation to the two white feet. Klīṃ, salutation to the two red-and-white feet. Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ, salutation to the two feet that are a mixture of red and white. Thus is the secret tetrad of feet.

And on the crown of the head, at the end of the *śrīgurupādukā* mantra, having recollected and performed the placement (*nyāsa*) in the left, right, middle, and all upper regions, as well as in the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus located at the *dvādaśānta*, one should place Gaṇeśa upon the *ādhāra*.

Having bowed to the Goddess together with her retinue in the heart by means of the root mantra, and having performed the purification of the palms, the three *tāla*-claps, the binding of the directions, and the construction of the fire-walls using the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*),
one should place the seed-syllables of Bālā at the navel, the heart, and between the eyebrows; then, touching the heart, [one should contemplate] her.
Having repeated this four times at the end, saying "O Śrī Tripureśvarī! Protect me," one should perform self-protection (*ātmarakṣā*).

Then, having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*)—consisting of exhalation and so forth—repeated three, six, and twelve times with the root-syllables, one should pervade [the body] four times with the root-syllables both collectively and individually.

Having produced the fourfold body— consisting of the subtle and gross bodies which are the common causes, and which have as their ultimate reality only the egg of power (*śakti-aṇḍa*), the egg of illusion (*māyā-aṇḍa*), the egg of primordial nature (*prakṛti-aṇḍa*), and the egg of earth (*pṛthvī-aṇḍa*)— and having performed the placement (*vinyāsa*) of the *mātṛkā* according to the root-syllables in both direct and reverse order;

Then, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) using the three seed-syllables in this sequence: from the navel up to the feet, from the heart up to the navel, and from the crown of the head down to the heart; likewise, on the palm of the left hand.
In the one called Dakṣa there are two, and the third belongs to both.

One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the crown of the head, the secret place, the heart, the three joints, the two ears, the mouth, the two shoulders, the back, the two elbows, and the navel region.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantra-syllables upon the body according to the sequence taught by the teacher, and having performed the placement of the six limbs and the triad beginning with the *ṛṣi*, one should remember: "Aiṃ is the seed-syllable, Sauḥ is the power (*śakti*), Klīṃ is the peg (*kīlaka*); this is the application (*viniyoga*) for the sake of attaining the grace of the goddess Śrī Tripurā. Then [one recites]: Āṃ Hrīṃ Kroṃ Ya-ra-la-va-śa-ṣa-sa-ha-l̥-kṣaḥ...

The vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of the venerable Goddess Tripurā are here; thus the life-force (*jīva*) of the venerable Goddess Tripurā is situated here. Thus may all the senses of the venerable Goddess Tripurā—speech, mind, sight, hearing, smell, and breath—having come here, remain happily for a long time. *Svāhā*. *Haṃsaḥ saṃ laṃ*. This is the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*).

Having formed the gestures of the rosary, the book, fearlessness, and the boon— reciting "Obeisance to the rosary, to the book, to fearlessness, to the boon-giver"— and having bound the *yonimudrā* with the syllable *aiṃ*,
one should meditate and worship according to the ritual procedure with sixteen or five mental offerings, using the mantra of dedication to Brahman (*brahmārpaṇa*).

Having performed the offering to Brahman (*brahmārpaṇa*) and the offering to the Self (*ātmārpaṇa*) with the *Anu* mantra, and having attained oneness with the Root Mantra (*mūla*), one should become the very embodiment of the deity oneself; then, taking the rosary received from the Guru—which has been smeared with fragrance and well-incensed—one should perform the recitation of the mantra (*mantrajapa*). And that [recitation] is as follows:
Recitation (*japa*) is of three kinds, distinguished as vocal, whispered, and mental. As it has been said:
"That which is performed with high, low, and circumflex tones, using distinct words, phrases, and syllables..."
One should utter the mantra with speech; that is the vocal sacrifice of recitation (japa-yajña).
One should recite the mantra slowly, moving the lips slightly;
one should know that when there is a faint sound produced by oneself, that is remembered as *upāṃśu* (whispered) recitation.
That meditation which proceeds from one syllable to another, from one word to the next,
through the practice of contemplating the meaning of the words— that is called mental recitation (mānasa-japa).

Thus [he says]. At the conclusion of the recitation (*japa*), having again visualized the Goddess as if she were separately present before him, he should say: "O Guardian of the most secret of secrets! Accept this recitation performed by me.
O Goddess, who dwells within my heart, may success be mine through your grace!"

Having thus offered the recitation at the base of the Goddess’s feet with this mantra, one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma), the three pervasions (vyāpaka), and the ritual placements (nyāsa) such as those for the limbs and the ṛṣis; this is the brief summary of the general procedure for the recitation of the Tripurā mantra.
The detailed account should be sought elsewhere. May there be auspiciousness! 6.

Regarding the question of how one should perform the *cintā* (meditative visualization) in the context of "it is contemplated" or "it is recited," [the author] speaks of the remaining *sakala* (manifest) form of the Goddess with the five verses beginning with "Vāma," since it has been taught that the *niṣkala* (unmanifest) form consists of light and speech, and because the form of the *sakala-niṣkala* (both manifest and unmanifest) type, such as that of Indra, has also been taught.
In verse:

She holds a book in her left hand and displays the gesture of fearlessness; in her right, she holds a rosary, her hand gracefully granting boons to her devotees, radiant as camphor and the kunda flower.
O Mother, how can those who do not contemplate you with their minds— gazing with eyes that possess the lovely luster of blooming lotus petals— ever possess the gift of poetry?

Regarding the word "vāma": O Mother! O Mother of the World! For those who do not cultivate You with their minds—that is, who do not meditate upon You—and who do not recite Your mantra with their speech, how could they possess poetic genius, far-sightedness, or omniscience? Not from any source whatsoever. But for those who, moreover, do cultivate You, how could there be an absence of poetic genius? Of what nature are You?

In her four hands, she holds a book in the left upper hand and displays the gesture of fearlessness (*abhayamudrā*) in the lower left; in the right upper hand she holds a crystal rosary, and the lower right hand is gracefully extended in the boon-granting gesture (*varadamudrā*) toward her devotees. She is radiant as camphor and the *kunda* flower.
Resplendent and shining like camphor and the *kunda* flower;
her eyes possess the luster of blooming lotus petals, and she gazes with a tender radiance— *ujjṛmbha* meaning "blooming" or "expanding."

(17) Of those eyes whose luster is like the splendor of the inner petal of a lotus— which is possessed of expansion by that [splendor]— [there is] one that is affectionate, moist with the essence of compassion, and endowed with radiance.
She possesses light, vision, and sight; she is to be seen as adorned with white garments, unguents, garlands, and ornaments, and bearing a crescent moon upon her mass of matted hair. || 7 ||

Having thus described the form to be meditated upon, which is common to the three seed-syllables, characterized by omniscience, and the fruit of its service, [the author] now describes the common form to be meditated upon and its fruit according to the sequence of Śakti, Kāmarāja, and Vāgbhava, within the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta), the mūlādhāra, and the heart-lotus.
Those who meditate on you stationed upon their heads, with a splendor as beautiful and clear as a cluster of white lotuses, as if sprinkling their heads with streams of nectar—
[from them] there issues incessantly from the interior of the mouth a flow of words consisting of blossoming and distinct syllables and phrases.
O Sarasvatī! Their speech is like the restless, trembling waves of the celestial river Gaṅgā.

"Those who [meditate on] you as Pāṇḍarā"—O Bhāratī! for those who meditate upon you stationed at their crown, the Goddess of Speech (Bhāratī) issues forth from the interior of their mouths without fatigue and without effort. Like the waves of the celestial river—*surasarit* being the Gaṅgā, and *kallola* its great billows—the waves (*ūrmi*) which are *lola*, meaning restless or flowing currents.
In the same way. Of what kind is the speech (*bhāratī*)? It is one whose syllables and words are blossoming and clear (*vikaca-sphuṭākṣara-padā*). "Blossoming" means not contracted;
"clear syllables" refers to those words which are capable of expressing their respective meanings and whose syllables are very lucid—it is thus described. Of what color do they meditate upon it?

She whose radiance was clear, white, and delightful like a mass of white lotuses—that is, a cluster of *pāṇḍarapuṇḍarīka* flowers—was such that her light was as bright and pleasing to the heart as a heap of white lotuses.
What was her activity? She seemed to be sprinkling the head of the practitioner with nectar-liquids dripping from her own limbs.
The word *iva* is used as a poetic ornament (*vākyālaṅkāra*).

One should meditate upon her whose radiant form bestows boons—such as a book and a rosary—upon the crown of the head; who consists of the essence of Śiva and Śakti; and whose splendor is white like a kunda flower or the moon. (8)
18) Having thus taught the form to be worshipped by those seeking the goal of speech and other such dharmas, [the author],
desiring now to teach the form to be meditated upon by those seeking sensual desires (*kāma*), sets forth the unique meditation on the second seed-syllable.
And he states the result:
"Those who [behold] this sky, covered by a mass of vermilion dust through your splendor, and even this earth, as if submerged in a spread of liquefied lac juice..."

Those whose minds are focused on nothing else for even a moment certainly become submissive to those who have eyes like those of a frightened young deer, though they may be exhausted by the fever of love.
"Ye sindūre..."— the vocative "O Bhāratī" is to be supplied here. [It refers to] the seed-syllable of Madana situated in the secret place, red as a hibiscus flower, dripping with red nectar.
Having reflected upon this and having applied it to the object to be accomplished, the clever person surely brings her under his control.

Because this has been favored by the Teachers (Ācāryas), because it will be stated in the subsequent verse as "those who [meditate on] you in the heart," and because no specific location is mentioned here, it is understood that this is meditation on the form situated upon the supporting lotus. Nor is there any contradiction with what precedes or follows; for just as there are specific types of worship (*upāsanā*), so too are there specific supports (*ādhāra*).
This is because it is intended for a specific purpose. Previously, meditation for the sake of omniscience was taught for all [seeds];
now, it is stated that each individual seed has dharma and so forth as its fruit—thus the distinction is established.
Furthermore, the foundational lotus possesses the nature of the Kāmagiri-pīṭha and is the abode of Kāmeśvarī.
The *Śrīsaubhāgyamārga* also corroborates this point: "O Bhāratī!

By whose splendor do people behold even for a moment this sky as if covered by a mass of vermilion powder, and the earth as if submerged in a spread of liquid lac, drenched in the juice of red dye? By what [splendor] of yours?

Having become single-minded with an undistracted mind, having sat down properly upon your own seat, and having withdrawn the defects through breath-control (prāṇāyāma), you— with your senses and mind withdrawn from their respective objects— [should meditate] upon you, whose form is entirely red and whose expansion of glorious radiance spreads in every direction.

The meaning is "having withdrawn [the senses]. Alternatively, those whose minds are not directed elsewhere, having ascertained you—such as you are—from their teacher, from the scriptures, and through direct experience, [meditate] upon you as their very own self.
Having thus taught the form to be cultivated by those seeking the goal of speech and other such qualities,
he now states the unique meditation and its fruit for the second seed-syllable, desiring to teach the form to be meditated upon by those seeking sensual pleasure (kāma).

For those whose minds are focused on nothing else for even a moment, who behold this sky as if covered by a mass of vermilion dust through your splendor, and this earth as if submerged in a spread of molten lac, the fever of the bodiless god (Aṅgaja) [is extinguished].
Those whose eyes resemble those of weary, trembling young fawns will certainly become submissive.

Regarding the phrase "ye sindūra": the vocative "O Bhāratī" is to be supplied. It refers to the seed-syllable of Madana (Kāmadeva) situated in the secret place, red as a hibiscus flower, dripping with red nectar.
Having reflected upon this and applied it to the object to be accomplished, the wise person surely brings her under control.

Because this has been thus favored by the Teachers, because it will be stated in the subsequent verse "those who [meditate on] You in the heart," and because no specific location is mentioned here, it is understood that this is meditation on the form residing within the supporting lotus. Nor is there any contradiction with what precedes or follows; for just as there are specific modes of worship (*upāsanā*), so too are there specific supports (*ādhāra*).
This is because it is intended for a specific purpose. Previously, meditation for the sake of omniscience was taught for all [seeds];
now, however, it is stated that each individual seed has dharma and so forth as its fruit—thus, the distinction is established.
Furthermore, the support-lotus possesses the nature of the Kāmagiri-pīṭha and the status of being the abode of Kāmeśvarī.
The *Śrīsaubhāgyamārga* also corroborates this point: "O Bhāratī!

By whose splendor do those who behold even for a moment this sky—the intermediate space—as if covered by a mass of vermilion powder, and the earth as if submerged in a spreading flow of liquid lac, as if drenched by a torrent of red dye? By what [splendor] of yours?

By what means [is this achieved]? Having become single-minded with an undistracted intellect, having sat down upon one's own seat according to the prescribed rule, and having removed all defects through breath-control (prāṇāyāma), one should withdraw the senses from their respective objects along with the mind. This is accomplished by you, whose entire form is a mass of radiant splendor, through the expansion of the light of your auspicious body that spreads in every direction, as you are of an exceedingly deep red color.

The meaning is "having withdrawn [the senses]. Alternatively, it means those whose minds are not directed elsewhere, who ascertain You—such as You are—from their teacher, from the scriptures, and through direct experience, as being none other than their own Self.

Now, he who worships another deity, thinking "He is one and I am another," does not know; for such a person is like an animal to the gods, as the Scripture censures the one who perceives duality. This is also logical: how could the world, consisting of men and women and submerged in the ocean of the body's radiance, belong to a deity other than the Self?

Likewise, how could it come under the control of the meditating person, or how could it itself attain direct perception within his heart? For it is universally accepted that there is indeed nothing other than the self existing inside the body; thus the logical proof is established. To the question, "What then of those [other elements]? he says: "Of those..."

Exhausted by the fever of love: when this [man] is heard of or seen, they become exhausted by the great heat—the fever—of the Love-god who has arisen within them in a hidden form, their bodies rendered helpless;
with eyes like those of a frightened young deer, meaning the eyes of a terrified fawn.

Those whose gaze is like that of a young deer—such women, beautiful in every limb, come under their control; even those women who are not entirely subject to kings who have brought the entire circle of the earth under their own sway do so. This is certain and beyond doubt.
The sense is that the direct experience of those devoted to you is the sole authority in this matter.

One should meditate upon her who resides in the lotus of the support (ādhāra), who is marked by the bow, arrow, boon-granting gesture, and gesture of fearlessness, who has the luster of a bandhūka flower, and whose nature is that of Kāmarāja. 9.

Having thus taught the fruit of the second seed-veneration, which is the attainment of all desires through the grasping of a distinguished object, [the author], desiring to instruct seekers in veneration,
now states the meditation and the fruit specific to the first seed:

O you whose mind is fixed on her! Those who, having made you steady, meditate upon you for even a moment— wearing shimmering golden earrings and armlets, with girdles and flower-garlands bound in place—
in their dwellings, the delights of amorous play expand daily for a long time.
Fortunes, as unsteady as the flapping ears of elephants in rut, attain stability [only] through [the support of] you.

"Cañcat" and so forth. Here too, the word "Bhāratī" (Speech) is to be supplied. Those who, having fixed you—having determined you—to be steady within their minds, that is, in the lotus of the heart, meditate upon you even for a moment, [meaning] they worship you as their own self.
And of what nature was she? She was one who wore trembling golden earrings and armlets—that is, she wore armlets together with two golden earrings that were swaying and shaking.
She was one by whom a girdle and a garland of golden lotuses had been bound.
Or [the one] whose girdle-string is fastened. Why is there a stabilization of consciousness? To this it is said:

"O Thou who art present therein always as the inner self of all beings!"—this is a qualifying vocative. In their dwellings, the fortunes—that is, the riches—attain long-lasting stability. Of what nature are they?

"Tremulous like the flapping ears of an elephant in rut" means they are as unsteady and unstable as the ears of an elephant intoxicated with passion; the sense is that even though they are inherently unstable, what do they do? Day after day (*aharahah*), they expand and increase. From what cause? From *vibhrama*, meaning from playful charm.
Because it manifests many forms such as land, gold, cattle, rice, barley, vehicles, jewels, garments, and so forth; or else,
because even those as flickering as the flapping of the ears of intoxicated elephants attain stability— thereby revealing the attainment of elephants, horses, and other such things.

One should meditate upon her who is the embodiment of Vāgbhava, shining like gold in the heart-lotus, radiant with the noose and goad, and holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in her hands. 10.

Now, desiring to teach the form to be meditated upon by those seeking liberation, he describes the unique meditation and its fruit for that previously mentioned partless syllable situated within the second seed-syllable—which he himself has taught as the *sārasvata* [mantra]—by virtue of its being an internal means for the knowledge of the reality of Sarasvatī: ...he says: [the following].

With playful grace, they meditate upon you— four-armed and three-eyed, with a mass of matted hair adorned by the crescent moon, wearing a garland of human skulls and garments as red as the Bandhūka flower, seated upon a corpse-throne, and possessing full, lofty breasts.
[He meditates] on the body marked with three folds in the middle, for the sake of realizing your true form. || 11 ||
Regarding the term *ārbhaṭyā*: here too, the word *bhāratī* is to be supplied. *Ārbhaṭyā* means by way of the *ārbhaṭikā* style.
Placing both thighs [together] while remaining on the thighs is the *ārbhaṭikā* posture (*āsana*).

By him [it is said]: she who is seated upon the *pretāsana* (the corpse-seat), having attained union (*saṅgata*) with Supreme Śiva—who has reached his own merger (*svamelana*) through excellence—she is that very *preta* (corpse) reclining comfortably upon the bed of Vāsuki;
that is the *pretāsana*, and she whose nature (*śīla*) it is to sit (*āsituṃ*) upon that, [is] she who dwells on the left lap of Śiva.

"Seated"—this means: they meditate upon you who are thus situated, for the sake of perceiving your form, that is, for the sake of accomplishing the direct realization of your true nature. Of what kind [are you]?
One whose mass of matted hair (*jaṭājūṭa*) is adorned with a crescent moon; that is, the mass of matted hair is adorned by a crescent moon (*śaśikhaṇḍa*), which is a digit of the moon.
She who possesses that [garland]: a garland of human skulls, or one like a jasmine wreath—consisting of human skulls or a string of large, round, white pearls—or one adorned with *campaka* flowers;
wearing garments as red as the blossoms of the *bandhūka*, or a garment (*ambara*) clothed in clothing as crimson as the *bandhūka* blossom.

"She who bears [the crescent moon] is thus; she has four arms, meaning she whose arms are four; she has three eyes, meaning she whose eyes are three; she has full and elevated breasts, meaning she whose breasts are full and high;
her body is marked by three folds that are sunken in the middle, meaning it is depressed and sunken in the central region."

One should meditate here upon the Goddess, who consists of the essence of the arts of love (kāmakalā), who is seated within the lotus of the heart, who is reddish-hued, whose body is marked by the three folds and is thus beautiful in every limb, and whose excellent arms hold the sugarcane bow, flowers, arrows, noose, and goad.
Alternatively, one should meditate on Śivā at the mūlādhāra with the vāgbhava syllable,
at the heart with the kāmabīja, and indeed at the center of the eyebrows with the final syllable.
One should meditate on the Goddess in the form of the *kāmakalā* at the *dvādaśānta*,
or one may meditate on her in the heart according to the path taught by the ancients.

The teachers have explained the meditation on the manifest (sakala) and unmanifest (niṣkala) forms as follows: one should meditate on [the deity] of reddish hue, endowed with a rosary, a book, and the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, like that of Indra;
having arisen within the solar disc, situated upon the support surrounded by petals.

For the pacification of suffering, the practitioner of mantra should meditate upon that which is called the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], which has the luster of the morning sun and is surrounded by a host of vowels, as it issues forth continuously from the cavity of his own mouth, enveloped in spreading rays of light.
(22) It arises within the interior of the *yoni* shining from the orb of the sun situated in the heart-lotus;
it possesses a radiance equal to the midday sun and is surrounded by the letters ending with *ka* and beginning with *pa*.
One should meditate upon the seed-syllable of King Manmatha, which agitates the entire universe;
by bestowing even Lakṣmī, who increases the sovereignty of kingship, one shall delight the world.

Then, having meditated upon the final seed-syllable (Aḥ) situated within the letter A, shining in the womb located at the end of the twelve finger-breadths above the head— the orb of the moon arisen there— enveloped by the pervasive vowels and possessing white luster;
and having bathed it with the pure nectar-water of Sarasvatī, one becomes a creator of divine poetry and the like.
The practitioner of mantra quickly destroys constant vomiting, untimely death, planetary afflictions, misfortunes, and physical disorders.
Thus it is said. Furthermore, the method for the recitation of each individual seed-syllable (*bīja*) has been graciously bestowed by the Teachers:

"He who, dwelling in a house made of earth, adorned with pure ornaments and possessing a clear luster, should recite the *Vāgbhava* syllable one hundred thousand times, having performed the fire-oblation (*homa*) consisting of a tenth part of that, and having muttered the mantra while using collyrium as the sacrificial material—"
He fills the entire world with his own poems that encompass manifold meanings; moreover, he is incessantly served by beautiful women who are overwhelmed by the pangs of love for him.
Clad in red attire, wearing a reddish-brown silk garment, and anointed with delightful saffron paste,

the practitioner of mantra, observing silence and comfortably seated upon the ground, should recite one hundred thousand times the seed-syllable consisting of the Lord of Rati (Kāmadeva), until the end of the prescribed fire-oblation.
He who exists in the world is served and honored by both gods and men.
Likewise, in a cellar, one who is self-controlled, adorned with white flowers, garments, ornaments, and ointments, should mutter the final mantra a hundred thousand times;
then eloquence shall issue incessantly from his mouth.
And the world, with its manifold paths of words, comes under his control.
Thus, the entire method of meditation upon the Goddess has been revealed by means of these five verses; may there be auspiciousness. 11.

"O Mother! For those who do not cultivate You with their minds, how can there be poetic genius? By this, it is stated that for those devoid of Your service, omniscience—and by the logic of the indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇanyāya*), all-encompassing sovereignty as well—is difficult to attain.

Now, He says that for Your servants, both of these are easily obtained even in this very world, even if they are very few in number: [The verse follows: *saṃsāre 'smiñ janani bahavo ye vipannā vipadyante vartante ca prabhavati na teṣāṃ bhavatyā vinā kaḥ | tasmāt sarveṣv api jananīti prathitā tvaṃ prasiddhyai tvatpādābjaṃ śaraṇam upayāmi prapannaikavandyam ||* In this worldly existence, O Mother, many have perished, are perishing, and continue to perish; yet there is no one who prevails without You. Therefore, You are celebrated as the "Mother" (*jananī*) among all beings for the sake of universal renown. Thus, I take refuge at Your lotus-feet, which are to be worshipped solely by those who have sought protection.

Though born into a family that was merely ordinary among kings and possessed of few attendants, he attained the status of a universal sovereign over the entire circle of the earth and became exalted by his majesty.
O Goddess! That Śrīvatsarāja became one whose feet are worshipped by hosts of Vidyādharas—this is the arising of grace born from prostrating at your lotus-feet.

"Born," [it is said]. O Goddess! This is that very thing born from prostrating at your lotus-feet—that is, arising from the act of bowing before your lotus-feet. It is the "dawn of grace"—the dawn, meaning the emergence, of your grace, which is your inclination toward bestowing favor.
The implication is that the elders declare this to be the very fruit of service to you. To the question, "What is it?"—it follows:

It was said: "Born," and so forth. There was a king named Śrīvatsarāja, who was born not merely in the lineage of ordinary kṣatriyas who have been consecrated as monarchs, but rather in that of regional rulers (māṇḍalika). Even there, he was born not into a family possessing abundant wealth, grain, livestock, retinues, fields, and so on, but rather into one with few possessions.
"Exalted by his majesty"— meaning, exalted by that majesty which causes fear to enemies even from afar—
and having attained a state of supreme eminence; "the sovereign of the entire circle of the earth"— meaning,
the sovereign who holds command over the whole earth extending to the four oceans.
Having attained— that is, having reached without effort— the station of that universal monarch (sārvabhauma), the sovereign of the entire circle of the earth,
his feet were saluted by hosts of Vidyādharas.
[The sciences (vidyās) consist of] the auxiliary branches (aṅgas), the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, and the extensive system of Nyāya.
The Purāṇas and the Dharmaśāstras—these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge.
Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, Gāndharvaveda, and thereafter Arthaśāstra; these are traditionally recorded as the eighteen branches of knowledge (vidyās).

Thus, in the Śrī Vāyavīya [Purāṇa], they have been taught: those who uphold them, recite them, hear them, bestow grace upon others, and personally practice their meaning according to their respective capacity—they are the Vidyādharas. He whose feet are saluted by their multitude, that is, by their assembly, is he whose two feet are worshipped.
Likewise, he himself became the foremost among those who had reached maturity in their respective sciences,
the protector and worshiper— meaning the leader— of the Vidyādharas, Brahmins, and others; thus he became both a sovereign emperor and omniscient.

24) That this is the connection [expressed by] "this is that. One should not explain [the term] *vidyādhara* as those possessing the sixty-four arts and sciences such as dance, song, and instrumental music, because that would suggest the king possesses only limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatā*). Nor...

The *vidyādharas* are those who are experts in the various divisions of the *Tripurā-vidyā*; [they are not mentioned here] because they lack devotion to the Supreme Deity, who embodies the forms of all deities for the king. Nor should it be explained that the *vidyādharas* are certain celestial beings (*vaimānika*) belonging to the divine class (*devayoni*) who occupy lower stations; [the reference is] to the "multitude" (*vṛnda*) of them.
For it is impossible for them to be servants of this sovereign while they are sporting in the divine state of the Vidyādharas;
therefore, the Śruti says: "This entire earth might be full of his wealth;
that is one human bliss. A hundred such human blisses are equal to one [bliss of the ancestors]."
"The bliss of humans and gandharvas," and so forth. || 12 ||
Now, explaining the meaning of the statement, "O Mother! how can there be poetic talent for those who do not cultivate you with their minds? he speaks of the fault in the contrary case:
"O Caṇḍī! for the sake of worshipping your lotus feet, [there is the gathering] of *bilva* leaves..."
How could those whose hands never came into contact with the sharp points of thorns become rulers of the earth,
their palms marked with the staff, goad, wheel, bow, thunderbolt, śrīvatsa, and fish,
and radiant like lotuses?

"O Caṇḍī! O fierce one! O you who are skilled in performing what is unpleasant for those people who do not turn away from your service! Here, for the sake of worshipping your lotus feet—for the purpose of adoring your lotus feet—the hands of those embodied beings [are wounded] by the tips of thorns breaking as they pluck bilva leaves—bilva leaves being *bilvapatrāṇi*—highly (*ud*)... [upwards].

Day after day, despite being subjected to extensive plundering and cutting, they did not undergo the familiar process of being scraped by the millions of tips of thorns that were breaking and being severed;
among leaves, there may be the *bilva* leaf, but no other leaf is superior.
The lotuses of the Hayamāra [mantra] become slightly blossomed.
Since the *puṣpa-vidhāna* (prescription for flowers) is mentioned in the scriptures, it is stated [therein] as "bilvīdala" (bilva leaf). How indeed are those kings born?
What are their characteristics? They are distinguished by hands marked with the *daṇḍa* (staff) and other signs, and possessing the luster of lotuses.

Or rather, the ellipsis is "how do poets arise"? In the phrase "the book on the left," sovereignty is indicated by means of omniscience; here, however, omniscience is [indicated] by means of sovereignty—this is the distinction. || 13 ||
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of worshipping the lotus-feet of You," in response to the inquiry as to who possesses the qualification for that worship of Your feet,
by what means it is performed, what characteristics the one to be worshipped possesses, what the fruit for Your worshippers is, or after how much time that fruit may arise, He says:

O Goddess Tripura! Having gratified you— who consist of both the supreme and the inferior— with milk, clarified butter, honey, and wine during the ritual of worship, the Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas,
and others surely obtain whatever their minds desire through your steady grace.
They swiftly attain their respective accomplishments, unhindered by obstacles. || 14 ||
"Brāhmaṇas, kings," and so forth. O Goddess Tripura!

Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, those other than them such as women, Śūdras, and those born of inverse unions (vilomaja)—all these, having gratified you, who consist of both the supreme and the inferior and whose form is both with parts and without parts, by means of milk and other offerings during the ritual procedure of worship—that is, the performance or method of worship—[attain their desires].

Having offered even a single drop of perfume, unbroken rice, and flowers, and having satisfied [the deity], whatever worldly or otherworldly accomplishment— whether small or great— their mind constantly prays for through its steadiness, that very thing is swiftly attained without being obstructed by obstacles, even when they have encountered them.

They attain [this] either in this very birth or in the immediately following birth; this is certain (*dhruvam*). The sense is that the direct experience (*svānubhava*) of your devotees is the proof (*māna*) in this matter. As they have said:
"Where there is worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*), there is no liberation (*mokṣa*); where there is liberation, there is no enjoyment."
For those intent upon the libation (tarpaṇa) of Śrī Śaṅkarī, both worldly enjoyment and liberation are truly held in the palm of their hand.
Thus it is said. It has also been graciously affirmed by the Blessed Lord:
"In this [path], there is no loss of effort, nor does any obstacle exist.
Even a very little of this dharma protects one from great fear."
Thus (p.
"O Pārtha! Neither here nor in the hereafter does destruction exist for him."
For no one who performs good deeds, my dear, ever goes to a state of misery.
Having attained the worlds of the doers of meritorious deeds and having dwelt there for countless years,
one who has fallen from yoga is reborn in the home of the pure and the prosperous.
And so forth. Regarding the doubt as to whether milk and the other items are each connected with all [the castes] beginning with the Brahmin,
or whether they are connected one by one with each caste beginning with the Brahmin respectively—
the latter is the case, because the worship of clarified butter (*ājya*) must necessarily be accepted by Brahmins, and the worship of milk (*kṣīra*) by Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas.
