The second position is tenable: the statement "A Brahmin shall not drink liquor" refers to those who are not initiated (*adīkṣita*), not to all Brahmins without exception. Therefore, as in the case of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, it is not a fault for a Brahmin to satisfy the Supreme Deity with liquor made from flour (*paiṣṭī*); thus, the first position should be accepted. Even in that regard—

All substances should be taken by everyone according to availability, according to capacity, according to intelligence, and according to inclination. For this very reason, the Śruti states: "One should hire a Brāhmaṇa who will drink the remnants.
Thus, because of the injunction that "one should eat what is desired and what remains," the Brāhmaṇa must perform the drinking of the *āsava*.

If it is argued that [the rule] has been attained, we say no; for even by smelling and consuming [the substance], as in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, the eating of what is desired and what remains is accomplished. Furthermore, this is because those established in the Kaula path accept that in the world, the base may become excellent and the excellent may become base. As was stated by Utpaladeva in the *Śrīmatstotrāvalī*:
Salutation to the Lord, who is contrary to the Vedas and Āgamas, who establishes the Vedas and Āgamas,
who is the true essence of the Vedas and Āgamas, and who is the secret one.
Thus it is said. Since the matter has already been thoroughly investigated by previous scholars, what is the use of our own effort?
For instance, their statement is as follows: "Because it contradicts all the scriptures, this does not deserve to be considered authoritative."
Moreover, because it is established by direct perception, the teaching proclaimed by Śiva is indeed a valid means of knowledge.
But this is the definitive conclusion here: that which is not authoritative for those who lack the qualification will be authoritative for those who possess the qualification.
In this matter, there is no qualified candidate, nor is any authority a determining factor;
generally, we do not accept either its status as established by direct perception or its being spoken by Śiva.
And so forth. Thus, it is fitting that all substances be accepted by everyone according to their availability, their capacity, and their preference.
This is the sequence of worship here: on a golden, silver, or copper plate, or upon a cloth marked with a lotus on the ground...

An eight-petaled lotus endowed with two-fold [concentric] enclosures; in its pericarp, the corners are supported by the fire, Varuṇa, and Īśa, joined to the middle of the fire-triangle situated between the two cities of Indra.
This wheel of nine sources, which is very difficult to obtain in the world, was ordained by the sages of old for the worship of the Goddess.

Having drawn the nine-yoni wheel with the characteristics thus described, and having consecrated a wooden pedestal— which is variegated, washed, smeared with fragrance, and well-perfumed— by means of ritual ablutions and other rites according to the rules, and having placed [the vessel] upon it,

one should perform the recitation (japa) according to the previously stated sequence; then, at the conclusion of the ritual placement (nyāsa), [one should place] a conch shell in front of oneself on the left side.

Having prepared the general *arghya* in a vessel of gold or similar material, and the special *arghya* to its right, one should [visualize] the lineage of the Śrīnāthas and the four secret feet upon one's own head; Gaṇeśvara in the *ādhāra*; and the Goddess together with her retinue in the heart by means of the root-vidyā.

Having gratified [the deity] with perfumes, unbroken grains, flowers, and drops of nectar (*amṛtabindu*), and having himself performed the manifestation of the three principles (*tattvatraya*), he should become the very body of the goddess Śrī Tripurā and begin the external worship (*bāhyapūjā*).
Herein lies the alternative arrangement of substances such as milk for the special offering (*viśeṣārghya*); this is the path of instruction (*upadeśādhvan*) in this context.

A Brāhmaṇa, having prepared well-boiled milk and having filled the special *arghya* vessel with that which has been turned into nectar (*amṛta*), should worship. In its absence, however, he should use clarified butter (*ājya*); in its absence, honey; in its absence, liquor (*āsava*); and in its absence, scented water (*gandhodaka*). A Kṣatriya, on the other hand, should use clarified butter, and in its absence, milk; in its absence, [the same sequence applies].

If that is unavailable, [the Brāhmaṇa should use] honey; if that is unavailable, liquor; if that is unavailable, fragrant water. A Vaiśya, however, [should use] honey; if that is unavailable, ghee; if that is unavailable, milk; if that is unavailable, liquor; if all are unavailable, fragrant water. A Śūdra, however, [should use] liquor; if that is unavailable, honey; if that is unavailable, clarified butter; if that is unavailable...

"By means of milk": since this is also the same for the offering of *arghya* with fragrant water when nothing else is available, this alone is the distinction here between the twice-born traveler of the right and the traveler of the left. What is that? When one satisfies the Supreme Deity with *āsava*, then at the end, the traveler of the right (*dakṣādhvaga*) should perform the mere smelling of it.

The manifestation of the three principles (*tattvatrayaprakāśana*) is indeed performed with scented water contained within a conch shell; however, the manifestation of the three principles and so forth by means of another [substance] must be performed with liquor (*āsava*) alone. Although this matter is not to be spoken of, nevertheless, because it must be stated even if it is highly secret during the investigation of the principles (*tattvacintā*), it has been declared by us. Now...
The procedure for external worship: On the left and right of the pedestal (pīṭha) are the Guru and Gaṇeśa.

Then, Kālāgnirudra, Ādhāraśakti, Ananta, Pṛthivī, Vidyā, the Ocean, the Boat, the Lotus-seat, the Discus-seat, Sarvatobhadra, the Maṇḍala, the Śrīcakra, the Throne, and the Seat of the Mothers—these, beginning with Kālāgnirudra, are to be worshipped with their own names in the dative case followed by "namaḥ."

One should worship Vidyābdhi and the others with the mantras of Śuddhā, Bālātripuravāsinī, Tripurāśrī, Tripurādevī, and Tripurāsiddhā; [one should place] Dharma and the other virtues as the four legs of the pedestal in the corners starting from the southeast, and Adharma and the other vices as its limbs in the four directions starting from the east.

Having worshipped with the glorious twelve-fold half-vidyā in the directions, and having worshipped a cushion of flowers upon that, and having worshipped Māyā-vidyā and the lotus upon that, one should worship the nine Śaktis on its petals and in the pericarp:
Icchā, Jñānā, Kriyā, Kāmī, and immediately after, Kāmadāyinī.
Rati, Ratipūrvā, Priyā, Nandā, and Manonmanī.
Then, within the central womb, [one should place] the nine wombs, the twelve powers (śakti), and the four seats (pīṭha):
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and likewise Sāmbikā; Icchā, Jñānā, Kriyā, Kubjikā, and Ravihvī (or Ravihvī) along with Saviṣagrikā.
Dūtarī, Sarvādyā, and the one named Nandā—these are the Śaktis;
one should worship them from the center to the end within the spaces between the lines and curves.

Aiṃ, obeisance to Kāmagiri-pīṭha; Klīṃ, obeisance to Jālandhara-pīṭha; Sauḥ, obeisance to Pūrṇagiri-pīṭha; Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ, obeisance to Oḍyāṇa-pīṭha—thus, within that, one should place the four pīṭhas in the centers of the three middle corners with Hrauḥ.

Having worshipped the pedestal with the mantra "Salutation to Sadāśiva-Preta-Padmasana" using scents, unbroken rice grains, flowers, and drops of nectar, and having offered incense and lamps, one should touch the form with the mantra "Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ,
salutation to the form of the Goddess Śrī Tripurā," and [meditate] upon it.
Having invoked the Goddess, who is of the nature of light, from one's own heart through the *ānanda-vidyā* by means of the *pravaha-nāḍī*, and having pervaded [her] with the *tri-bālā*;

At the conclusion of the nyāsa of the letters, the mantras, and the limbs, one should perform— as previously described— the nyāsa of the sages (ṛṣi) and so forth, the consecration of life-force (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), and the display of mudrās; then, having bowed, one should offer a seat, welcome, water for the feet (pādya), water for honor (arghya), and water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) using the seed-syllables of Bālā and the others.
The honey-mixture, a bath once again, a pair of garments, and ornaments.

Having thus offered the ritual honors (*upacāra*), one should worship [the deity] three times with the second seed-syllable using the petals and other parts; then, having bestowed the nectar-drop (*amṛtabindu*) seven times, twenty-seven times, or three times with the third seed-syllable, one should perform the worship of the retinue with permission. [The offerings are:
"Homage to the rosary," "To the book of knowledge," "To the one who grants fearlessness," and "To the one who grants boons"—thus for the weapons.
Furthermore, upon the lotus-hands of the Goddess, one should place the first Guru’s sandals; on the lotus-feet of the Goddess, the remaining [sandals];

and behind the Goddess, in the space between the eastern and central *yoni*s, one should generally place those for Parā, Aparā, and Parāparā, and specifically, in front of that, the triad beginning with Anantanātha and one's own two Gurus.
One should worship [the deities] as being in the east and west; and on the two sides, Rati and Prīti, and in front, Manobhava;
and in the four directions—namely, southeast, northeast, southwest, and northwest—in due order.
One should worship the six limbs within the space between the central yoni;
on both sides of the central yoni, two by two, and five in front.
One should worship the five arrows, beginning with *drāṃ*, *drīṃ*, *klīṃ*, *blūṃ*, and *saḥ*;
they are [the powers of] drying (*śoṣaṇa*), deluding (*mohana*), inflaming (*sandīpana*), heating (*tāpana*), and exhilarating (*mādana*).
The Bāṇas should be known as ending with the fourth [letter], each having its own numerical value as its form;
Subhagā, Bhagā, and at the end of those, Bhagasarpiṇī.
Bagā and Mālinī are to be worshipped in sequence within the directions and the sources;
likewise, Anaṅgā, Anaṅgakusumā, and Anaṅgamekhalā.
Anaṅgamadanā should also be worshipped in the womb-angles (koṇayoni). Brahmāṇī is to be worshipped with Asitāṅga, and Māheśī together with Ruru.
Kaumārī together with the wrathful deity known as Caṇḍa, Vaiṣṇavī with Unmatta, Vārāhī with Kapālī, and Indrāṇī [with her consort].
One should worship Bhīṣaṇā on [one] petal and Cāmuṇḍī on [another], as well as Caṇḍikā with Saṃhāra; indeed,
one should worship these upon the petals using their own names in the dative case.
Āṃ to Brahmāṇī, Aṃ to Asitāṅgabhairava, and so forth.
Again, [one should worship] Indra and the others in the directions, and then the vajra and other [emblems] outside;
thus, having worshipped the retinue with scents, unbroken rice, flowers, and drops of nectar upon the form of the Goddess—

Having offered a handful of flowers with forty-four mantras, having presented incense and lamps, and having performed the *ārātrika* rite, one should offer the oblation of boiled *śāli* rice accompanied by sugar and side-dishes of plantains and coconuts mixed with ghee; then, having performed the fire ritual (*agnikārya*), [recites] *oṃ hrīṃ*.

Having scattered the *bali* offering with the mantra "To all beings who create obstacles, *huṃ svāhā*," and having bowed, given the nectar of water (*pānīyāmṛta*), and dismissed the food offering (*nivedya*), one should give to her [the goddess] with the mantra "Aiṃ! O Ucchiṣṭacaṇḍālī! Mātaṅgī!
O you who bring all under control, *svāhā*," and then, having given the mouth-rinsing water (*gaṇḍūṣa*) and so forth, perform the propitiatory worship (*prasannapūjā*).
Having performed the offering to Brahman (*brahmārpaṇa*) and the offering of oneself (*ātmārpaṇa*), having accepted the sacred site (*tīrtha*), having offered praise and prostration,

having become one with that [deity] himself, having performed the limb of dissolution (*layāṅga*), and having dissolved [the deity] within himself, he should perform the consecration of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) and offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) once each to his own self and to the form of the Goddess.

Having worshipped the conch and placed it [there], and having recited the mantra at the appropriate time according to one's inclination—preceded by the *aṅga-nyāsa*, *ṛṣi-nyāsa*, and so forth—and having performed the yogic practices, one should become identical with the deity; may there be auspiciousness! 14.

Regarding the phrase "consisting of the high and the low," in response to the inquiry as to what that supreme form of the Goddess is and what her inferior form is, he first describes the supreme form:
"In this world, you are called Vāgvādinī, the mother of all sounds."
From you indeed Keśava, Vāsava, and the others certainly manifest;
and at the end of a kalpa, even Brahmā and the rest surely dissolve into you.
Thus, you are praised as a certain supreme Śakti of inconceivable form and majesty. 15.
"You are the mother of words here"—O Vāgvādinī!

[The term] *vāgvādinī* refers to one whose nature (*śīla*) is to cause the organ of speech (*vāc*) to speak; thus is the address. Likewise, O Sarasvatī! here in this world consisting of word and meaning, you are called by the wise the "mother of words."
Because it has evolved into the nature of the fifty phonemes through the sequence beginning with Parā and Paśyantī, [it is the source] of all things characterized by the Vedas and so forth.
And because words are composed of that [Brahman]. We do not say it is exactly so;

rather, Keśava, Vāsava, and the like—whether as Keśava and others, or as Vāsava and others—are indeed primary referents, yet they manifest from you at the beginning of a kalpa. How much more so, then, other objects? This is certain.

This is certain because meaning is a transformation (*vivarta*) of the word. As they say: "Brahman, which is without beginning or end, is the imperishable essence of sound (*śabdatattva*); it manifests as the form of meaning, from which the process of the world proceeds."

Thus [it is said]. Alternatively, because of the scriptural hearing that "In the beginning this was indeed undifferentiated; it became differentiated by name and form," and because it is established that sound originates from You, it is understood that the object also manifests from You alone. This is the meaning.

"Keśava and the others" refers to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva, who perform the fivefold cosmic functions beginning with creation. "Vāsava and the others" refers to the created beings—gods, humans, and so forth—as well as beasts, birds, reptiles, and stationary objects. Now, [one might object] that because they are immortal...
To the question of how there can be birth for Keśava and others, or Vāsava and others, who are devoid of destruction, it is said:

"In whom indeed these beings beginning with Brahmā, and those beginning with Vāsava, dissolve at the end of a kalpa. Their immortality consists solely in having a lifespan lasting until the end of a kalpa, not in being eternal. This is because they are subject to the activities of the world's creation and so forth.

The intention is as follows: since it is impossible for there to be sentient beings who are the creators of those [worlds], and because all [beings] are of the same nature as you, their destruction is possible through the destruction of their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), even though there is no destruction of their essential nature (*svarūpa*). Regarding origination, [the text says] "from Keśava comes Brahmā" (or "Keśava resounds together with..."), and regarding dissolution, "Brahmā."
The reading "Keśave" is an inversion. And it is said in the *Sakalajananīstava*:
"Like rays in the sun, like sparks of its flame, like droplets in the ocean whose majesty is formidable with its waves..."
O Mother! Rising again and again, along with their own essential families, the multitudes of principles, being subject to another's will, undergo dissolution within you at every kalpa.
Thus, O Mother! as named Viriñci you create; as named Hari you protect the three worlds; as named Rudra you destroy; and you bestow the state of Īśvara.

O Daughter of the Mountain! You exist as the one called Sādākhya, and you alone become manifold through the various distinctions of your creative powers by shattering the flood of bonds for the sake of bestowing auspiciousness.

And thus [it is said]: "You are she who generates this manifold expansion of words and meanings; because you transcend both word and meaning, you are profound with an inconceivable form. By the inconceivable...
By your form, which consists of indivisible bliss and consciousness, you are profound and difficult to comprehend;
you are praised as a certain supreme power (*māheśvarī śakti*), the most excellent of all.
Of him [the Lord], neither effect nor instrument exists; neither one equal to him nor one superior to him is seen.
"His power is indeed heard to be manifold. If it is argued, "Well then, since Śiva, the possessor of power, exists separately even during dissolution, his non-duality is not established," we say no.
This is because there is no difference between power and the possessor of power; for indeed, no one perceives a difference between sesame seeds and their oil, or the like.
For this very reason, it was said by the ancient sages:
"The wise declare that Śiva and Śakti are indeed one single reality."
Without Śiva there is no Goddess, and without the Goddess there is no Śiva;
there is not the slightest difference between the two, just as there is none between the moon and its moonlight.

And so forth. Here, within this single reality—which consists of Śiva and Śakti, whose ultimate essence is pure consciousness and bliss, or which takes the form of light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—one should understand the distinction that in the doctrine of the non-duality of consciousness (*saṃvidadvaitavāda*), conventional usage proceeds with emphasis on Śakti, whereas in the doctrine of the non-duality of the Lord (*īśvarādvaitavāda*), it proceeds with emphasis on the Possessor of Power (*śaktimat*). Thus, she is called Vāgvādinī.
By means of the invocation, the mantra of Śrī Vāgīśvarī should be understood to have been extracted through the citation of its opening words:
*vadavada vāgvādinī svāhā*.
The sage (*muni*) and other attributes for this mantra—Kaṇva, Virāṭ, and Vāgīśvarī—are to be applied in their respective order.
One should perform the six [limbs] beginning with the *aṅga*, situated within the short and long vowels and the consonants (*hal*).
This is the intended meaning of this verse:
[the sequence consists of] Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Śuddhavidyā, Māyā, Kāla, Kalā, Vidyā, Rāga, Niyati, Puruṣa, Prakṛti,
Ahaṃkāra, Buddhi, Manas, Śrotra, Tvak, Cakṣus, Jihvā, Ghrāṇa, Vāk, Pāṇi, Pāda, Pāyu, Upastha.

Sound, touch, form, taste, smell, ether, air, fire, water, and earth—these are the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*). This entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), consisting of words and their meanings, is composed of nothing but these. And they [the principles] are rooted in that single principle known as Śiva and Śakti, which is a dense mass of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss (*saccidānanda*).

By the analogy of the city of the mirage, they appear and disappear; yet that very reality always shines within all beings as "I am," even though it remains in its own form as a mass of consciousness and bliss.

It does not manifest [as a separate entity], but rather solely as the intellect (buddhi), the vital breath (prāṇa), and the body (deha) within emptiness (śūnya). It appears as "I am ignorant" through the intellect's state of emptiness;
as "I am happy" or "I am miserable" through the state of the intellect; as "I am hungry" or "I am thirsty" through the vital breath;
and as "I am fat" or "I am thin" through the body. Māyā is the cause for this manifestation as the emptiness of reality (tattva-śūnyatā).

Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) is the cause for manifestation through one's own essential nature. Through these two, there is bondage and liberation for this [Self]: bondage by *māyā* and liberation by *vidyā*. In that regard, although the Supreme Lord is satisfied by the experience of the bliss of his own nature, when he desires to manifest himself alone as the universe consisting of words and meanings, then he is Śiva.

That power of His is *icchā-śakti* (the power of will), because His will is unimpeded. At that very moment, suddenly perceiving through *śuddhavidyā* (pure knowledge) the universe—which, though already existing within His own self as if it were present—manifesting as "I am this," He beholds it as His very own self;
thus He is Sadāśiva, who perceives "I am this" just as one sees the reflection of one's own body in the middle of well-water.

Seeing his own self as if separate from pure knowledge (śuddhavidyā), he is Īśvara; therefore, through these two states, there is indeed the experience of the bliss of liberation. When he perceives the universe and the Lord of the Universe as entirely separate from himself due to Māyā, then he is Puruṣa, because [Māyā] is the cause for the appearance of impermanence even in that which is eternal.
Time is that which appears as such within Him. *Kalā* is the cause for the All-doer to become a doer of only some things;

*avidyā* is the cause for the All-knowing to become a knower of only some things; *rāga* is the cause for the Stainless One to become attached to objects; and [the sense of] "this is mine" or "this is not mine" pertains even to the Omnipresent One.
Necessity (*niyati*) is the cause of restriction. This group of six coverings (*kañcuka*), beginning with *kāla* and ending with *niyati*, is said to be accompanied by *māyā*;
they are so called because they cause the contraction of the *puruṣa*. And this sequence of contraction is as follows:
when the Lord, by means of His own *māyā*, [makes] the universe—which appears as if separate from Himself—[appear as such].

When, relying on the quality of *rajas* through the designation of *prakṛti*, he creates separately by means of the sequence beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*), then he is Hiraṇyagarbha as the Creator. When, acting as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) in that very same [state], he enters by relying on the quality of *sattva* and governs, then he is Viṣṇu. He is indeed that same one.
When [Prakṛti] withdraws [the universe] by resorting to the quality of tamas, she is then Rudra. Thus, Prakṛti consists of the three qualities (guṇas).
That very same [Prakṛti], her qualities agitated by the power of Īśa known as Parā, creates the Mahat-tattva in accordance with time and karma. From that [comes] the Ahaṃ-tattva; from that...
Having become the ego (ahaṅkāra), it creates the pentad of sound and so forth, the pentad of ether and so forth, the ten sense organs, and the internal organ; therein, first,
it creates the internal organ called mind, intellect, and ego, which consists of the powers of will, knowledge, and action, and then the instruments that are the means for knowledge and action.
Then, from that [intellect], it creates the five objects of cognition— sound and so forth— as well as their substrata, the five elements beginning with space. Thus...

The principles beginning with Mahat, created by the will of the Lord, join together in the course of time and produce the golden cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). When that egg, which rests upon the causal waters, has matured and split open due to His entry into it, the Puruṣa possessing a thousand heads and other attributes comes into being. Of him—

From the navel-lotus arises Hiraṇyagarbha. Having created the fourteen worlds and the beings contained within them—divided into four classes according to whether they are born from a womb, an egg, sweat, or a sprout—he enters into them.
Through his own *māyā*, he undergoes contraction by time and other factors and becomes a bound soul (*paśu*). He who...
He is called a god, an asura, a human, or a denizen of hell.

Bound by the contraction of the body and so forth, he wanders upwards, downwards, and within this world due to the merit and demerit produced by that [contraction]. The causes for the emergence of his body are indeed the principles beginning with Mahat. Therefore, when he—

Distressed by *saṃsāra*, he approaches a supreme guru who knows reality; having received the initiation of mantra from him, he worships his own self as the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). Then, by His grace, [he dissolves] the body into the cosmic egg (*piṇḍa* into *maṇḍa*), the cosmic egg into the earth, the earth into water, water into fire, that into air, that into ether, that into the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*), and that into the Great Principle (*mahat*).

Having withdrawn that *prakṛti* into *prakṛti*, that [prakṛti] along with its effects into *vidyā*, that [vidyā] into Īśvara, and even that [Īśvara] into the principle consisting of Śiva and Śakti—[I am] Brahmā, the creator of the universe;
Viṣṇu, the protector; Rudra, the destroyer; Īśvara, the concealer; and Sadāśiva, the bestower of grace upon all.

When one directly perceives that all beings, including gods and asuras, who occupy positions such as those of the emanated [sṛjya], are indeed myself alone, and that throughout the three periods of time there exists no other reality distinct from me; and when one perceives that I am none other than Paramaśiva— whose very body is a mass of eternal bliss and consciousness, embraced by the Supreme Power (parā-śakti), and not a mere human semblance— then [one attains] the Supreme Power.
Having abandoned her other form, she has attained identity with Paramaśiva and delights therein; and the person (pumān) becomes liberated.
Thus, both this state of bondage and the state of liberation have been revealed here. May there be auspiciousness! 15.

Having thus taught for the sake of the knowledge of reality the supreme form of the Goddess, which transcends the manifold expansion consisting of sound and meaning, he now teaches another form for the sake of worship:
"The triad of the gods, the three Vedas, the three fires, the triad of powers, the three vowels..."
The three worlds, the three steps, the three Puṣkaras, the three Vedas, the three castes,
and whatever object in the universe is regulated in a threefold way and consists of the three aims of life—
all that truly follows the name "Tripurā" in you, O Blessed One, according to reality. (16)
p.
35) "The triad of the gods is the Trayī. O Blessed One! [You are the embodiment] of complete sovereignty, heroism, fame, and splendor.
And because of knowledge and dispassion, as well as these six qualities, there is the designation "Bhagavat."

She in whom this sixfold group beginning with sovereignty (aiśvarya) always exists in its entirety is the Blessed Lady (Bhagavatī); such is the address to her. Whatever in the world is regulated in three ways, fashioned as the three aims of life (trivarga), or is a thing inherently of three forms—all that is in truth your name, "Tripurā. Its state is "tattva" (the true nature).

Therefore, because she possesses that very nature, she "follows," meaning she conforms to or expresses it; this is precisely what he states with the words beginning "of the gods" (*devānām*). It refers to the triad of the gods—namely, the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas; or Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya;
or Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; or the fire-eaters (*hutabhujām*).
The triad refers to the three fires—the *gārhapatya*, *anvāhārya*, and *āhavanīya*—or alternatively, the three fires of the earth, the stomach, and the submarine fire (*vaḍavāmukha*).

The *trayī* refers to the three Vedas. The *triśakti* consists of the powers of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*). The *trisvara* are the three accents: acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), and circumflex (*svarita*). The *trailokya* refers to the three worlds: *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*. The *tripadī* is the *gāyatrī* meter.
The *upavīta* is so called because it brings about *puṣkara*, that is, nourishment (*puṣṭi*) and satisfaction (*tṛpti*), for the three—namely, the gods, the sages, and the ancestors.

It is the "Triple Brahman" (*tribrahma*), meaning the threefold Brahman, which is the *praṇava*; or else, it refers to the Self (*ātman*), the Inner Self (*antarātman*), and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). This is according to the Lord’s own words: "My womb is the Great Brahman; therein I place the germ."

Or, primordial nature (*prakṛti*) exists as threefold through the distinction of the qualities (*guṇa*) such as *sattva*, being the triple Brahman; or the three castes situated in the *tāra* [syllable *om*], or those contained within this mantra; or the letters *a*, *i*, and *u* situated in the script;
or the letters pervading vowels and consonants; or white, red, and black, which are the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya.

Or rather, what need is there for much? Whatever in the world is regulated in three ways, consisting of the three aims of life (trivarga), all that truly corresponds to your name "Tripurā"—this is how it should be construed. By the word "whatever" (yatkiñcit), one should understand the triad of dharma and so forth, the triad of waking and so forth, the triad of morning and so forth, the triad of Suṣumṇā and so forth, the triad of the Vyāhṛtis, and the triad of time.

The triad of persons, the triad of genders, the triad of numbers, the triad of causes, the triad beginning with fire, and so forth are included. Thus, the supreme and inferior form of the Goddess— consisting of both word and meaning, yet transcending both because she is their cause, and having the nature of self-luminous, indivisible bliss and consciousness— is here [described] by means of these two.
It has been elucidated by means of two verses; may there be auspiciousness!

Thus, the meaning of the word *Tripurā*, the mantra, the deity, and the reality (*tattva*) have been explained here—from the beginning through the text already traversed—both in summary and in detail. And that [teaching] is for those seeking the fourfold aims of human life, without distinction between women and men.

It has been stated that [the practice] is to be well-served by all castes (*varṇa*), because even a single seed-syllable yields great fruit and because it constitutes a distinct mantra; furthermore, no one can perform worship if the prescribed substances are unavailable.

Regarding the items to be abandoned, many substances have been taught; among them, by the reading "kṣīra-ājya" (milk and ghee), the primacy of milk is revealed according to the maxim that "among Brahmins, kings," and "that which is more venerable comes first. This applies to the worship of Śivā with the fourfold offerings of solid food, soft food, that to be licked, and that to be drunk.

The predominance of the liquid substance and the subordinate status of the other ingredients are indicated by the use of the term "liquid substances" (*dravadravya*) and the word "satiating drink" (*tarpaṇa*). [The ingredients are:
saffron, agallochum, camphor, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), and sandalwood.
The wise should grasp the eightfold fragrance from the power (śakti) accompanied by the kacora-plant.
And this has been included by the Noble Ones everywhere under the mention of the flower "bilvīdalā," because it is recited together with them. || 16 ||

Since [the goddess] has been described primarily in this way, and because the various manifestations (*vibhūti*) of the Goddess have not been mentioned in the section concerning her with attributes (*saguṇapakṣa*), [the author],
while revealing the names of the Goddess that correspond to her various functions and purposes, first states the unique fruit associated specifically with the name "Tripurā":
One should remember Lakṣmī in the royal court, Jayā at the front of battle, Kṣemaṅkarī on the road, Śabarī in the mountain fastnesses of the forest infested with carnivorous beasts,
elephants, and serpents, and Mahābhairavī when there is fear of ghosts, spirits, piśācas, and jambhakas.
In times of delusion, they cross over calamities by means of Tripurā, and in a flood of waters, by means of Tārā.

"Fortune in the royal court," and so forth. The word "Bhagavatī" (the Blessed One) is to be supplied [to the end of the verse]. [The meaning is: you, though present in the royal court, being destitute of the appropriate implements, attendants, residence, and so on, and even while possessing all this, being oppressed by rival kings who are more powerful—[we worship] you, Lakṣmī, the Great Fortune, thus addressed.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: those standing at the front of battle, being oppressed by their adversaries, cross over calamities and abandon them by remembering you, Jayā, the Goddess Jayā, under that name. "Kravyādadvipasarpabhāji" means possessing carnivorous beasts, elephants, and serpents; "kravyāda" refers to wolves, tigers, and the like.
Having recollected you, the Goddess Kṣemaṅkarī, by that name, on a path infested with lions, elephants, and serpents;

In a forest, on a difficult mountain, and on a path hard to traverse— that is, in a forest and on a mountain that is inaccessible and steep to climb— by remembering you, who are Śabarī by name and possess the form of a Śabara woman; [and] in the fear arising from spirits, ghosts, piśācas, and jambhakas—
where *bhūtas* are the attendants of Rudra, *pretas* are ghosts, *piśācas* are demons, and *jambhakas* are rākṣasas.

Having remembered you as Mahābhairavī by that name; having remembered you as Tripurā by that name when delusion—that is, a confusion of the intellect—has arisen; or when a flood of water has occurred, meaning upon reaching a boat—a raft, a float, or a vessel—standing in the midst of a mass of water, having remembered you as Tārā by that name.
By remembering [these names], one overcomes calamities. We shall clarify the method for reciting these seven names later on. || 17 ||
Now he describes another form of the Goddess, consisting of the recitation of mantras:
Māyā, Kuṇḍalinī, Kriyā, Madhumatī, Kālī, Kalā, Mālinī, Mātaṅgī, Vijayā, Jayā, Bhagavatī, Devī, Śivā, and Śāmbhavī.

You are Śakti, the beloved of Śaṅkara; you are the three-eyed one, Vāgvādinī, Bhairavī, and Hrīṅkārī; you are Tripurā, consisting of both the supreme and the non-supreme; you are the Mother, and you are Kumārī. 18.

"Mayā-kuṇḍalinī"—here too, the word "Bhagavatī" (the Blessed Lady) is to be supplied. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that all those forms of words beginning with "Māyā" and ending with "Kumārī" are "Thou. *Hrīṃ* is Māyā;
*Aiṃ* is Kuṇḍalinī; *Klīṃ* is Kriyā; Madhumatī is Mātṛkā, both pure (*śuddhā*), with the nasal bindu (*sabindukā*), and with the visarga (*savisargā*).

The ten names are Kālī, Kalā, Mālinī, Mātaṅgī, Vijayā, Jayā, Bhagavatī, Devī, Śivā, and Śāmbhavī. The power (śakti) is the third seed-syllable of the venerable Bālā. The beloved of Śaṅkara is the power of Rudra.
When the Tripurā-vidyā, accompanied by the letters *ha* and *sa* and eternally situated with the letter *sa*, is without parts (*niṣkalā*) within the second seed-syllable.

It occurs. [In the word] *bhoje*, then *hrasī* is also extracted. The three-eyed one (*trinayanā*) is the seed-syllable of Kāma (*kāmabīja*), because of the presence of the eyes in the limbs born from the jewel (*maṇija*). Vāgvādinī is Vāgīśvarī;
she is indeed extracted as "you are the mother of all sounds" (*śabdānāṃ jananī tvam*). Here, Bhairavī is the five-peaked one (*pañcakūṭaka*).
That has indeed been extracted. The seed-syllable of Hrīṅkārī, the sovereign of the worlds, has been extracted in its own essential form.

Tripurā is the Śrīsaubhāgyavidyā. The mantra of Śiva-Śakti, consisting of both the supreme and the non-supreme, has also been extracted, because it constitutes the third seed-syllable of the middle four-peaked Tripurāśrīmantra.

The Mother is the illustrious twelvefold Vidyā; she too was extracted at the beginning. That maiden is the young girl (Bālā), who was extracted through direct perception itself. Although the Saubhāgyavidyā had not been extracted previously, [it is now extracted].

Nevertheless, she is revealed in this very verse. How so? By the double mention of *māyā* as *hrīṅkārī*, the repetition indicates the recurrence of the seed-syllable of the Lord of the World (*bhuvanādhipati*). Likewise, the double mention of *trinayana* indicates the recurrence of the seed-syllable of Kāma.
By the phrase *parāparamayī*, both *ha* and *sa* are included. When mentioned thrice, *māyā* and the syllable of Kāma are accompanied by *ha* and *sa*.

And it is not merely the *saubhāgyavidyā*; the letter *ai* is also included by the word *kuṇḍalinī*, because it is contained within *ai*. Since the vowel *ai* arises from the combination of the vowel *e* with the letter *a* (the *vṛddhi* of *e*), the form *aikāra* is produced. Alternatively, that [mantra] has already been extracted in the very first verse. How so? Because it was extracted as a six-peaked (*ṣaṭkūṭa*) mantra.

Furthermore, because all the syllables of the *vidyā* mantras are included therein, and with the intention that almost all mantras manifest within this very [Vidyā], the word "Mother" (*mātṛ*) is applied to her;
this is also due to the fact that this deity is named Tripurāmbikā. Thus, ten mantras have been described. Of these...

Through their mutual conjunction, the recitation of the mantra (*mantrapārāyaṇa*) comes about. It is as follows: *hrīṃ a kālī sauḥ*—this is the first mantra. Among these three seed-syllables (*bīja*), the first seed-syllable is the fourfold Mother-Scripture (*mātṛkā*) consisting of the pure and other letters; it is the first name among the ten names, and it is the first mantra among the ten mantras.

It is as follows: in the pure *mātṛkā*, there are fifty mantras beginning with *hrīṃ ā kālī sauḥ* and ending with *hrīṃ kṣa kālī sauḥ*. Likewise, there are fifty in the [mātṛkā] with the nasal bindu (*anunāsika*), beginning with *hrīṃ aṃ kālī sauḥ*. And in the [mātṛkā] with the visarga, beginning with *hrīṃ aḥ kālī sauḥ*.

There are fifty [mantras] containing the *sabindu* (the nasal bindu) within [the syllables] such as *hrīṃ aḥ kālī sauḥ*. There are also fifty [mantras] endowed with both the *bindu* and the *visarga* in [the syllables] such as *hrīṃ aḥ kālī sauḥ*. Thus, there are two hundred mantras. Furthermore, having substituted the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable (*aiṃ*) in place of the *māyā* seed-syllable (*hrīṃ*), and having performed everything else exactly as before—

Two hundred. Again, having placed the third seed-syllable of Kāma at the beginning and performing everything else exactly as before, there are another two hundred; thus, there are six hundred mantras. Again, having substituted the names of the *kalās* in place of the names of Kālī and performing everything else exactly as before, there are another six hundred. In this manner, for each name.

There are six thousand divisions. Furthermore, by substituting Śaṅkaravallabhā in place of the first mantra called Śakti, and having made everything else exactly as in the Vāgvada, [one obtains another set].

"Six thousand [times] *hrīṃ a kālī hsrīṃ*, and so forth. Thus, for each mantra, there are sixty thousand mantras. Now, another method: by joining the three seed-syllables with the fourfold Mātṛkā, when six hundred mantras have been produced under the name Kālī, while remaining within that very name, [one recites] the second of the mantras..."

In the *yojanā* [method of application] as well, there are six hundred mantras. Likewise, in the *yojanā* of the third mantra and so forth, there are six hundred for each; thus, when all the mantras are joined with the names of Kālī, they become six thousand designators.
Similarly, when joined with the names beginning with *kalā*, there would likewise be sixty thousand mantras here as well. Previously...

According to this principle, the recitation (japa) of the names such as Lakṣmī mentioned in the verse should also be performed, beginning with *hrīṃ a lakṣmī sauḥ* and so forth. Furthermore, by joining ten mantras for each name, there are forty-two thousand mantras in total. Thus, the complete recitation (mantrapārāyaṇa) amounts to sixty-two thousand plus one hundred thousand [recitations].
Auspiciousness. || 18 ||

Now he states the *Nāmapārāyaṇa*: "With the consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *kṣa*, joined with the vowels from *ā* to *ī* in pairs, then again with those same consonants from *ka* to *kṣa* joined with the vowels from *a* to *ā*."
O Tripurā! To those names of yours which are indeed extremely secret—O Consort of Bhairava! salutations to you who transcend the twenty thousand [names]. || 19 ||

"Ā ī pallavitair iti": O Bhairavapatnī! "Bhairava" is Maheśvara, whose nature is the light that devours the entire manifold of duality (*sarvadvaitaprapañca*). His consort is the radiance known as Parāśakti, who is his very essence, who has him as her sole support, and who delights in him alone; such is the address to her: "O Bhairavapatnī! Thus: "Ā ī."

Salutations to those thirty-five names of yours— beginning with the letters from *ka* to *kṣa*, preceded by the syllable *ā ī* as an opening prefix— which are extremely secret, numbering more than twenty thousand, specifically sixty hundred above twenty thousand.

The meaning is this: even your names alone deserve salutation because they bestow fruits upon the reciter even without meditation; how much more so, then, for you, whose wealth is your name! By what kind of syllables?
By those beginning with the vowels and ending with the letter *kṣa*, divided sixteenfold, starting from the first vowel and extending to the letter *kṣa*.

One should recite [the mantra] by proceeding in pairs of two syllables, joined with one another, beginning with *a kā ī* and ending with *aḥ kā ī*, and likewise from *a khā ī*, *a gā ī*, *a ghā ī*, and so forth, ending with *aḥ kṣā ī*.

There would be five hundred and sixty-six mantras. Then, by joining those very thirty-five syllables with the vowels in forms such as *ka*, *kā*, *ki*, *kī*, and so forth, there arise five hundred and sixty mantras for each one, beginning with *kakā-ī*, *kākā-ī*, and so on up to *kakhā-ī*.
From *kākhā-ī* and so forth, up to *kakṣā-ī*, *kākṣā-ī*, and so forth, ending with *kaḥkṣā-ī*;
likewise from *khakā-ī* and so forth, ending with *khaḥ kṣā-ī*; and similarly from *gakā-ī* and so forth, ending with *gaḥ kṣā-ī*.
Thus, even that which consists of the *nāmapārāyaṇa* has been revealed as another form of the Goddess. May there be auspiciousness! (19)
Having thus concluded the praise, he states that this [work] should be practiced by the virtuous: "This praise should be understood skillfully by the wise, having fixed their minds upon it;
for in the first verse, the name 'Tripurā' appears clearly in the word *bhāratyāḥ*, provided one is single-minded."

The procedure for the extraction of mantras has been explained according to the sequence of one, two, and three quarters, consisting of as many syllables as there are quarters, accompanied by specific details and endowed with the authentic tradition. || 20 ||
"It should be understood skillfully. Here too, the phrase "the wife of Bhairava" is to be supplied.

*Stuti* (praise) is speech that generates a sense of wonder within oneself—expressing "Oh, what excellence! Oh, what excellence!"—by describing the flow of the deity's qualities. This is a praise of the renowned *Bhāratī* known as Tripurā; it should be understood by the wise, those possessed of discernment, as being directed toward her.

Having fixed your mind skillfully upon that Bhāratī, you must understand her thoroughly and hold her firmly in mind. In this regard, being the subject of Tripurā-Bhāratī is one reason; he states another reason as well: "in which," meaning in which hymn, one is "single-minded," such that the mind is not elsewhere but in this very [hymn].

For that person, regarding him, in the first verse (the first *śloka*) of the initial composition, by means of syllables equal in number to his own feet—that is, by syllables possessing a count identical to the number of his feet; the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is used here in the sense of "being thus" (*itthambhāve*). By virtue of having an equal number of syllables, [the sequence follows] the order of one, two, or three feet.
The method for extracting the mantra has been explained and established according to the sequence of the first, second, and third quarters.

The meaning is that the Śrībālā mantra is extracted such that its first syllable occurs in the first quarter, its second syllable in the second quarter, and its third syllable in the third quarter. Of what nature is it?

"Accompanied by particulars" means accompanied by the specific mantras of Tripurā; the meaning is that the particulars have been extracted from it in some manner. "Clearly" means extracted through direct perception.

"Endowed with the true tradition" (*satsampradāyānvita*) means that this "true tradition" (*sat-sampradāya*)—being both faultless (*san*) and a lineage of instruction (*upadeśaparamparā*)—is what it is endowed with (*anvita*), that is, joined with. It has been obtained by me through the lineage of instruction from the best of gurus;
it was not fabricated recently, such that there might be a suspicion of its lack of authority due to being of human origin (*pauruṣeyatayā*).

The meaning is that only those mantras obtained through the traditional lineage have been extracted by us here. For everything can indeed be known only with an attentive mind; thus, it is said to be "taught to one who is single-minded. Furthermore, "one who is single-minded" (*ananyamanas*) refers to one whose mind thinks, "I am none other than Bhāratī, but she herself"; for such a person as myself...

The meaning is that [the commentary] was composed by me in such a manner as to be connected [to the original]. Thus, it has been stated that because of its purity in terms of its author, its subject matter, and its essential nature, it must necessarily be respected by the learned; may there be auspiciousness! || 20 ||
If it be argued that, despite its faultlessness,

this work should not be studied by connoisseurs because it lacks an abundance of verbal ornaments and because it is not a vessel for the nectar of sentiments such as the erotic (śṛṅgāra), let it be so— it need not be honored by them. Nevertheless:

Because devotion to the Supreme Deity is paramount, and because [this work] has arisen from me solely by the power of that devotion, those devoted to the deity will certainly accept it. Therefore, he says that this hymn is indeed fruitful:
"Whether it be flawed or flawless, what is the use of such consideration?"
Surely those who possess devotion to you will recite this hymn;
for even though I was firmly aware of my own insignificance, I have certainly composed it by force, having been made eloquent through devotion to you.

"Whether it be faulty or faultless," and so forth. O Consort of Bhairava! O Tripurā!—these forms of address should also be understood here. Let this [work] be faulty (*sāvadya*), meaning possessed of defects, or rather, let it be faultless (*niravadya*), meaning devoid of defects;
whether it be joined with the defects of lacking ornamentation or poetic flavor, or whether it be free from them—what is the use of such concern?

Or rather, there is no purpose whatsoever. Why? Because that person who possesses devotion toward you will recite this hymn; this is certainly and surely so. And why is that? Because you are intent upon composing a hymn for me, your own self; therefore, from the very moment of such an effort to accomplish an impossible task, [the result follows].

While remaining silent, having firmly contemplated and understood with certainty that lightness and the nature of the cognition of appearances arise within me, [I remain] through devotion to you— that devotion toward you which consists of unsurpassed love.

By me— who, though of little learning, have been made talkative, rendered loquacious, and set in motion by a flow of speech— this has certainly and undeniably been composed with force and speed, even without prior reflection. "Undeniably" (nirbādham) means...
Furthermore, even the defects of being devoid of ornament (*alaṅkāra*) and lack of aesthetic flavor (*sārasatva*) do not exist in this hymn when it is subjected to critical examination. Why?

Because the essence consisting of Śiva and Śakti—which is heard in the Śruti as the "most flavorful among flavors" (*rasānāṃ rasatama*)—is of the nature of indivisible bliss and consciousness; and so too is the rasa of devotion to Him.

This is because, while [the sentiment of] wonder (*adbhuta*) is manifested here as the predominant element throughout, the other sentiments (*rasas*) are also manifested as ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) by virtue of being subordinate to this [predominant one], as appropriate to each case. For instance, in the phrase "O Eternal One! [Your] agitation," there is the manifestation of wonder; and in the statement "Even a child is wise," there is the manifestation of pathos (*karuṇa*).

Regarding the phrase *yatsadyo vacasām*, it is stated that the wonder (*adbhuta*) of the vowel *au* becomes expressive of Sarasvatī when accompanied by the letter *ga*, whereas in its absence, it constitutes a mantra; thus, for the wonder (*adbhuta*) of "each one of yours" (*ekaikaṃ tava*), there is the book on the left (*vāme pustaka*); for the peaceful (*śānta*) [sentiment], "those who you, O pale one" (*ye tvāṃ pāṇḍare*); and for the erotic-in-separation (*vipralambha-śṛṅgāra*), "those who, O vermilion-colored one" (*ye sindūre*).

In the verse beginning with "cañcatkāñcana," the first half-verse expresses the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and the marvelous (*adbhuta*), while the latter half-verse expresses the heroic-exuberant (*ārbhaṭī*).
In "jāto'pi," the erotic-in-enjoyment (*sambhoga-śṛṅgāra*) and the tranquil (*śānta*) are expressed. In "caṇḍi! tvaccaraṇāmbuja," the fearsome (*bhayānaka*) is expressed.
In "viprāḥ kṣoṇibhuja," the pathetic (*karuṇa*) is expressed. [This applies] to all castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramiṇām*).
Because it is understood that the Blessed Lady, being worshipped with any substance whatsoever— regardless of whether it is male or female— as it may be obtained, grants each respective desire,
she is perceived as possessing supreme compassion; thus,
through the first and second halves [of the verse], she is the "Mother of Words" for the gods [in the context of] the marvelous and the terrifying.

The triad [of sentiments] is also present because the power of devouring all objects, known as Tripura, has been manifested; however, in the phrases "Lakṣmī in the royal family" and "Māyā Kuṇḍalinī," there is only the state of the Furious (bhayānaka) sentiment at the end and the beginning respectively, and no other rasa exists here.
It is made clear that since the work begins with the sentiment of devotion (bhaktirasa) and concludes with that very same sentiment, its primary purport lies therein.

Furthermore, while the figure of speech known as simile (upamālaṅkāra) occurs here and there in the first verses and elsewhere, there are also verbal ornaments (śabdālaṅkāra) such as alliteration (anuprāsa) and softness of sound (saukumārya).

Furthermore, its status as *citrakāvya* (poetry of striking artistry) is evident to the learned through its possession of concealed intentions (*gūḍhayojanatva*), concealed word-meanings (*gūḍhavarṇatva*), and so forth.
Thus, it is established that because it is free from defects, endowed with poetic qualities (*guṇa*), and full of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), this [text] should be studied by all.
Alternatively, these mantras taught here are considered non-human (*apauruṣeya*) because they are eternal, having been received through an unbroken lineage of gurus since time immemorial.
[All cognitions] are to be apprehended as intrinsically valid; however, this hymn which has just been spoken by you is not so, because it is of human origin (pauruṣeyatva).

There is no determination of validity, or even if there were such a determination, there would be no self-evident ascertainment of validity by which all people might accept this; to this he replies: "It is faulty" (*sāvadyam*). "Faulty" (*sāvadyam*) means that which exists together with *avadya*—that is, with defect (*doṣa*) or invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*). Alternatively, let this [position] be faultless (*niravadyam*). What is the use of such deliberation? This [deliberation] is not [necessary].

The meaning is that one should reflect upon this. Why? To this he says: "Certainly" (*nūnam*). That person who possesses devotion toward you and has fallen on the side of theists will recite this hymn;
the meaning is that for him, this [hymn] will certainly become a source of valid knowledge (*svataḥ-pramāṇa*) by itself. He establishes that very point with the words: "In oneself" (*ātmani*).

Perceiving that this matter was beyond human power, I—a man of little knowledge who had desisted from the effort of composition upon reflecting on the lightness [of the task]—have nonetheless been made vocal by my devotion to you;
and through service to you, my intellect has been awakened by You, who have manifested as my very self. Thus...

And by this very manifestation of the flow of speech, it has been firmly and eternally composed and revealed—forcibly and without effort—not, however, produced now by the play of our own intellects. Therefore, the meaning is that the learned should accept this as a source of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in its own right. [This was stated] by the author with respect to himself.
It should be understood that the common designation "Laghustuti" (Short Praise) arose because the word *laghu* (short/light) was employed;

or, it is called *Laghustuti* because it is composed of twenty verses, despite its extensive meaning due to its rapid composition; or, it is the *Laghustuti* because it is the praise (*stuti*) of the Goddess who is *laghu*—that is, straightforward and non-deceptive toward her devotees. || 21 ||
Thus, this hymn of praise to Śāradā, composed by the Laghubhaṭṭārakas in twenty-one verses, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon devotees.

By the grace of the lordly sage Kṛṣṇānanda, he who attained the fourth stage of life (turyāśrama) as a state free from exertion, and having realized the Self through his own self as established at the pinnacle of the Vedas,
and having also received the Śiva-filled manual (paddhati) from the Guru Ānandanātha—
The sage Rāghava, who brings joy to the end [of suffering], arrived; he provided sustenance until satiety.
I bow to that single Supreme Reality which is proclaimed as Kṛṣṇa, the Three-eyed One, the Consort of Tripura, or Brahmā— He whose singular body is existence, consciousness, and bliss.
To the Universal Self, for the tearing asunder of all bonds.
This work is completed.
May there be auspiciousness.
